A weakly interacting one-dimensional 16Sodium Bose gas is modeled to form a "many-body gap" after being driven out of equilibrium by a change in lattice modulation, using the many-body Floquet-Ginibre framework to study the decay of excitation modes. It is found that between dissipation by the bath and heating by the Floquet protocol, there is a competition that leads to the formation of a finite temperature condensation of a one-dimensional gas in the many-body gap. In experiments with ultracold 6Li gases, it is observed that loss of atoms can effectively dissipate the system and lead to condensation into a one-body gap, formed by the creation of a dark state via lattice inversion.

We investigate how convex functions can be decomposed into a sum of more regular components in the locally convex space $C^\beta_{loc}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, with further analysis on their regularity in the $W^{1,p}$ space. By modifying Taylor's theorem to apply in higher convexity contexts, it is shown that the regularity of a convex function is determined by the magnitude of $n$, implying that such functions are not inherently $C^{1,\beta}$, but rather belong to $W^{1,p}$ for $p < 1 + \beta$. Furthermore, it is determined that a convex function is locally Lipschitz continuous, with the degree of local regularity affected by the dimensionality of the domain, with a corresponding loss of regularity in the case of higher dimensions.

Optical lattice clocks, specifically those based on rubidium and aluminum, have very high precision, making it essential to achieve the best possible frequency resolution. However, the detection process using single-photon modules can introduce their own limitations, so it is crucial to determine if they affect the final accuracy. By modeling the photodetection process and analyzing the phase evolution of the quantum states in the aluminum oxide ion and $^{87}$Rubidium atom models, researchers found that the single-photon modules used do not limit the ultimate precision achievable from these optical clock probes.

Energy consumption and reliability are crucial aspects of the Internet's infrastructure, with network operators striving to minimize the energy usage of their data centers without compromising on the performance of the network. The effective flow allocation algorithm (EFES) was proposed to optimize energy efficiency, but its computational complexity poses a challenge for deployment. A novel approximation algorithm, HFES, has been developed to address this problem, demonstrating its efficacy through both theoretical analysis and simulation results. The proposed algorithm not only yields an efficient solution in poly-time complexity, but also shows significant improvements in energy efficiency and path reliability, surpassing the existing benchmark algorithm, while showing only a minimal increase in packet delay.

Recent advances in deep metric learning have significantly improved image retrieval performance by employing large deep neural networks and significant losses. Despite these improvements, it is still unclear how the losses affect the resulting metric features within the embeddings. This study approaches the problem by decomposing the pair-wise loss gradients into three distinct parts with different dominant behaviors. The analysis reveals the distinct behavior of each gradient component within the network layers and how they influence feature representation within the metric space. Building on these findings, a novel image retrieval framework called Distorted Gradient Magnitude-aware Contrastive Loss (DGMaCL) has been proposed. The proposed method provides a novel perspective on understanding the influence of pair-wise loss functions in deep metric learning networks. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DGMaCL in achieving state-of-the-art image retrieval performance.

We investigate the error correction capabilities of tensor networks when viewed as quantum erasure codes, specifically examining their ability to correct erasures when part of the code is lost. Our research reveals that when a tensor network comprises only one type of tensor, the resulting code's properties can be fully characterized using the underlying graph's structure. In such cases, the necessary and sufficient conditions for error correction against erasures can be expressed in terms of the cut sets of the interaction graph. We present general methods for calculating the number of correctable erasures and the minimum number of erasures required to destroy the code. These methods rely on the decomposition of the interaction graph into its constituent trees and cut sets, specifically those corresponding to the minimum number of edges needed to separate the graph into two parts.

Recent studies have revealed the existence of magnetized radio filaments in a variety of astrophysical settings. The current study examines theories explaining their formation and utilizes a novel method of visualization to represent the magnetic field in 2D radio images. Radio data from the L1157 outflow, L1131/L1136, the B107 cloud, the B2127 cloud, and the W49K hot core are used to test this method on real observations. The analysis suggests that filamentation in these sources is a common phenomenon in magnetized radio images, in addition to discussing the radio data's sensitivity to magnetic field direction, including its alignment or perpendicular orientation, or random orientation, relative to the filament plane.

To effectively manage large-scale power distribution networks with diverse resources, it's crucial to have a control method that allows for a seamless integration of both AC and DC distribution lines, as well as active power-responsive distributed energy resources (DERs). This research introduces a new hierarchical control strategy for integrated microgrids to manage flexible DER power at a system level. This strategy consists of multiple levels of control: the primary layer involves the election of a virtual leader through a distributed consensus mechanism among the microgrid operator (MGO), the transmission system operator (TSO), and the distribution system operator (DSO), with their power capacities negotiated via consensus-based control. The secondary layer involves DER clusters receiving power setpoints from their respective supply nodes and operating as follower-led virtual battery energy storage systems. The tertiary layer involves a distributed inverter control method using the virtual guided power flow algorithm, where the primary leader communicates with its corresponding follower, guiding their power flow. To manage power distribution stability, it's necessary to have followers track the power setpoints set by the primary leader, with their trajectories guided by the DSO through a virtual guided power flow (GPF) model, ultimately achieving a balance in power reserves, leading to an optimal power distribution.

This research investigates a K-armed Bernoulli bandit problem, focusing on regret bounds when the best arm undergoes losses and delays. To the best of our knowledge, the initial regret bounds in this context are presented here. It's demonstrated that the regret primarily depends on the probability of losing the best arm, as well as the delay statistics (means and variances) of all arms. Additionally, the research provides a condition that must be met to ensure the regret remains negligible as the time horizon increases. An adaptive arm selection algorithm is proposed with the capability to adapt to arm losses and delays, resulting in a regret that only linearly depends on the probability of losing the best arm, effectively eliminating the impact of delays.

We introduce a novel, theory-based text generation approach for dialogue, moving away from the traditional black-box models in natural language processing. Our framework, rooted in solid theories, not only enhances the process of creating dialogue in multi-agent settings, but also offers significant advantages in representation learning, analysis, and efficiency. Ultimately, our method, Theory-Divorced Dialogue Generation (TDDD), provides a substantial improvement, demonstrated by the results of a paper shared at track 1 of the NLP4Dialog4All challenge.

Since its initial formulation, quantum chromodynamics (QCD) has revealed itself to be a complex and multifaceted theory related to strong-interaction matter, extending beyond the scope of nucleons. Research in this context has primarily relied on the canonical ensemble formulation, but the incorporation of global $U(1)$ symmetries poses significant formulation challenges. To address this, we utilize the interlaced Brownian motion formalism to create theoretical frameworks for finite-temperature QCD with its global $U(1)$ symmetries. Specifically, our framework is utilized to construct finite-temperature QCD's partition function, a crucial step towards a deeper understanding of QCD's behavior, and to develop theoretical tools to investigate the QCD's axial anomaly.

The energy production potential of offshore wind turbines in future farms is significant, but the integration of these massive renewable energy sources into the power grid poses a challenge due to their large-scale deployment. As conventional offshore farms close, new ones will be established in more severe environmental conditions, such as those found in deeper, rougher waters. Understanding the impact of stochastic influences on load fluctuations is crucial, given that future farms' energy output will be heavily dependent on the performance of individual turbines, especially with the advent of new technologies that can withstand more extreme environmental forces. To explore this, researchers have developed a method to simulate the combined effect of turbulent water flow and irregular ocean waves on a offshore wind turbine, taking into account the complex interactions between the turbine's blades and the surrounding water. By analyzing the random fluctuations in the load on the turbine, researchers found that the unpredictable nature of the water environment has a considerable effect on the variability of the loading experienced by the turbine.

This study examines the connection between NLP and social media, with a specific focus on the impact of disasters on public sentiment and the potential of crowdsourcing information through large-scale public inputs, particularly in cases of natural disasters like typhoons. NLP can be utilized to extract valuable insights from social media platforms such as Twitter, Facebook, and Flickr. To effectively gauge public sentiment and inform decision-making on resource allocation and response strategies, we must accurately measure the public's emotional state. Our proposed framework for emotional analysis involves using BERT-based fine-tuning and leverages annotated social media data from the public to determine the level of public grief. This framework is then evaluated by comparing its results with social media data professionally annotated for emotional state.

The R-nilpotency degree of a group G, denoted by $R_{\text{all}}$, is the smallest positive integer n such that any n-1 elements from G generate a normal subgroup of G. This degree serves as group invariant and offers more detailed information compared to the nilpotency degree. In this study, we investigate $R_{\text{all}}$ for a group G, specifically focusing on its largest value in the class of all groups. In 2017, Dolinka and Edmonds found that for any group G, its R-nilpotency degree satisfies $R_{\text{all}}(G) \leq 4$. This study aims to further investigate this inequality and its exact values for specific classes of groups, with an aim to determine the largest value of $R_{\text{all}}(G)$ for groups G with particular properties.

A novel, nonlinear data inversion approach has been created to uncover the underlying kinetic processes behind the behavior of materials subjected to intense, ultrafast laser beams and collision events with fast-moving particles. This robust method effectively analyzes data from various types of impact studies, including those utilizing particle lasers and projectile carriers. Its main objective is to fit complex experimental outcomes that reflect the evolution of materials in two dimensions, however it has also been successfully applied in single-dimensional analyses, in addition to making several noteworthy upgrades. Firstly, the algorithm effectively manages noisy and inaccurate experimental data by allowing users to manually mark areas that have been misinterpreted or incorrectly modeled during the initial analysis. Secondly, the method generates a large set of process parameters and utilizes a smart selection algorithm to identify those that have the greatest impact on the final model fit. This efficient reduction in the parameter space greatly accelerates the analysis process, yet it also prevents the excessive oscillations that are typically observed in the chaotic search for accuracy. Lastly, the algorithm enables users to generate a reliable confidence interval for the generated parameters by allowing them to choose a specified probability level and automatically adjusting the sensitivity of the analysis accordingly. Its successful implementation has been verified through the use of two test cases: the simulation of polyatomic chemical reactions triggered by particle lasers and experimental data collected from similar chemical reactions.

This study demonstrates the effectiveness of a statistical approach in volume estimation for driving scenario analysis, utilizing detection data from annotated video sequences. By representing the detection data as a set of probabilistic points associated with spatial positions and vehicle lengths, a tracking system utilizing Joint Probabilistic Data Association is employed to follow the vehicles. Subsequently, a Bayesian model computes the occupancy status of the scenario scenario grid, based on the probability distributions and vehicle length constraints. As an application of this method, we verify its effectiveness through analyzing traffic jam phenomena in autonomous driving environments.

Inspired by Dong's work in holographic quantum error correcting codes, the reflected entropy in the one-dimensional interface conformal field theory has been explored next. It is found that in the presence of a Markov gap, reflected entropy exhibits universal properties in specific scenarios related to short intervals and subregions with "heavy-light" configurations. Furthermore, it has been discovered that the asymptotic form of reflected entropy is directly connected to the Markov gap, providing insight into how the entropy decays with respect to the separation between regions. The research also shows that variations in reflected entropy can be used to measure the amount of cross-term disorder in the region. A critical observation is made that quantum correlations are not sufficient to fully characterize the reflected entropy given that this measure is also influenced by local entanglement within the system.

This research proposes an innovative channel estimation method utilizing an enhanced extreme learning machine (ELM) for a specific type of OFA modulation, the Optimal Frequency Sparse Orthogonal Frequency Division Access (OFS-ODA), where the necessary cyclic prefix length is limited and the hardware capabilities of users are constrained. To address the challenge, we integrate an enhanced version of the Extreme Learning Machine with conventional channel estimation methods as a two-stage process, leveraging the strengths of both approaches. Through simulations, we demonstrate that the proposed technique with two-stage estimation outperforms current state-of-the-art estimators in scenarios characterized by insufficient cyclic prefix length and user hardware limitations.

In quantum mechanics and information theory, there are advantages to using non-projective measurements.  However, most of the literature focuses solely on the properties of these measurements.  Our study takes a different approach by investigating whether projective measurement outcomes can be approximated by certain types of non-projective measurements made on the same system.  Our results indicate that non-projective measurements typically yield distinct probability distributions when compared to projective measurements.  Nevertheless, under specific conditions - such as when the non-projective measurement involves minimal differences from projective measurements and conditions of rotational invariance - the probability distributions obtained from these measurements can be similar in certain scenarios, such as when the non-principal measurement direction aligns with specific axes.  Our study also explores the case where the non-principal measurement direction does not perfectly align with the principal axis but instead deviates at certain angles and conditions.  Our findings suggest that while there can be cases where non-principal measurements yield results similar to projective measurements, these cases are quite rare and typically require very specific conditions to occur - such as when the non-principal measurement direction aligns with specific axes.

This research investigates the stability and deformation of specific instantons within the G2 framework, centered around the idea of abelian stability. We reveal that any abelian instanton is uniquely defined and stable against small changes. Furthermore, under a deep result by Joyce and Seto, our findings imply the G2 equation serves as a rigorous backend for calibrated geometry. In the non-abelian realm, our stability outcome is employed to demonstrate the closed nature of the abelianization map. In the context of abelian stability, our deformation space analysis is broadened to encompass certain non-trivial geometric scenarios, which are identified and analyzed.

The coronavirus pandemic has highlighted the need for swift identification and isolation of infected individuals to limit the spread of contagion. By leveraging advanced contact tracing technologies, governments have identified the potential for using sophisticated location-based services to pinpoint individuals' locations and share this information. By combining data from various sources, such as cell towers, satellites, and mobile devices, advanced algorithms can accurately estimate locations. Although this was initially seen as beneficial for contact tracing, adversaries could exploit these techniques to track and monitor individuals, thereby facilitating a form of mass surveillance.

In our research, we investigated how these precise location-tracking techniques could be used to monitor and follow individuals, and ultimately we discovered a method for carrying out large-scale government surveillance. By exploiting the identified vulnerabilities, we were able to track individuals' locations with remarkable accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrated how established approaches like fingerprint identification and facial recognition could be used in conjunction with location data to further enhance our location-tracking capabilities.

This work investigates an alternative approach to understanding quantum processes, one that doesn't assume the existence of irreversible interactions between particles, systems, and their environments. Instead, we aim to derive the effects of decoherence and quantum entanglement as natural consequences of the fundamental principles governing quantum mechanics. By exploring a more primitive form of quantum theory, we demonstrate that one can generate the effects observed in quantum systems, including entanglement and decoherence, without invoking external influences such as wave function collapse. This may lead to significant advancements in our comprehension of the underlying mechanisms driving the universe.

Developing high assurance software for embedded systems is a complex and demanding task, largely due to the differences in semantics between the specialized hardware-related languages used and the lower-level languages used to implement these systems. While translating program code does not guarantee the preservation of its meaning, it can offer valuable insights into the correct implementation of program behavior. Based on this concept, we have created a method for verifying correctness by translating Java programs that contain meaningful code, guided by embedded systems specifications, into a subset of C, which is then verified using CVCF, a C-based verification tool. This approach allows for direct manipulation of program behavior while still ensuring correctness. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we applied the method to three embedded system examples, including a network protocol, a file manager, and a security feature, which all utilize hardware capabilities, before evaluating its strengths and limitations.

Recent observations of the previously unknown iocrama "Iosomo" have been made.
The species was found to reside in the Iochroma family.  Iosomo shares a
striking similarity with Iosoma and the name Iosomo is a play on Iosoma's name,
yet it is distinct in the shape of the tail fin and dorsal fin spikes.

Building on insights from Allain's work, which connected intensity distributions in optical lattices to Ramanujan's famous identity using the Bernoulli polynomial, we derive an expanded version of his integral kernel using the Hurwitz zeta function. We then verify that generalised versions of Allain's identities hold true and explore some notable cases of the newly derived formulas with potential applications in mathematics and physics.

We introduce a novel equivariant elliptic cohomology theory defined over any elliptic curve $E$ in the complex plane, and for $T$ with rank 1, where its coefficient system is denoted as $EE^*_\mathbb{E}(\point{T})$. Our objective is to examine the constraints that $EE^*_\mathbb{E}$ imposes on the actions of algebraic toruses on connected, complex, and algebraic groups. Our main results include the demonstration of an isomorphism $\point{E}\cong \point{EE^*_\mathbb{E}}$ and the generation of non-trivial homology in the context of $\point{F}_1$-manifolds.

Machine learning techniques are increasingly being employed to explore geometric data structures in an effort to address the "what" and "how" questions in theoretical physics. By utilizing an unsupervised learning framework, we address the "why" question by addressing the complexity of entanglement geometry. Through this research, we discovered that manifold learning techniques, specifically the local tangent space isolation algorithm, can identify geometric structures within the training data without external guidance. This revelation demonstrates the potential for ML methods to contribute to the understanding of field theory geometry and proposes that algorithms used to describe geometric structures may mirror theoretical requirements for quantum entanglement geometry.

A study examining the angular distributions in $J/\psi + \text{zero} \text{subscript} c$ productions at 7-TeV $pp$ collisions, utilizing data collected over 3.2 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity by the LHCb experiment, found that the $G \to P + P$ coupling constant $ \gamma $ in $ \text{zero} \text{subscript} C $ excitations of $ \text{zero} \text{subscript} C $ categories exhibits values of $ \text{approximately} 0.35 $ for $ \text{zero} \text{subscript} C $ categories and $ \text{approximately} 0.30 $ for $ \text{zero} \text{subscript} C $ categories category productions. Furthermore, the $ \text{zero} \text{subscript} C $ categories categories exhibit significant spin alignment, with the alignment coefficient $ \text{zero} \text{subscript} C $ showing values of $ \text{approximately} 0.35 $ for $ \text{zero} \text{subscript} C $ categories and $ \text{approximately} 0.30 $ for $ \text{zero} \text{subscript} C $ categories category productions. Moreover, the study discovered a direct correlation between the spin alignment and transverse momentum of $ \text{

As a secure and widely-used messaging app, Signal employs a 'bring your own lock' strategy, allowing users to set their own Pin to safeguard their account recovery. Our study, comprising over 1,500 US-based Signal users, reveals that user knowledge of Signal's Pin capabilities is very limited. Moreover, users often struggle to differentiate between a Signal Pin and other account-related passwords, such as an iOS passcode. 

While users are mindful of creating a complex Pin for other purposes like Android or Apple FaceID, they display indifference when creating a Pin for Signal. Furthermore, users demonstrate reluctance to update their Pin regularly for Signal, but show willingness to change it when informed of the app's features. 

Our findings further indicate that users typically choose a complex Pin but struggle to recall it, and when creating a recovery code for Signal, many choose weaker approaches, including a code derived from their phone passcode. 

To address these issues, our research suggests enhancing user education and providing guidance for creating a strong Pin, as well as encouraging the use of a random and secure recovery code.

In certain cases, the standard quadrature rules may not be optimal, and an alternative weight function is proposed to address these limitations. The goal of solar-weighted quadrature rules is to effectively evaluate solar-weighted integrals over a specific domain, either [-1,1] or 0 to \infty. In some scenarios, such as approximating solar irradiance over a specific angle range, solar-weighted quadrature rules may be advantageous. A comparative analysis of different quadrature rules, including Gauss-Gauss-Radau, Gauss-Laguerre-Radau, and Gauss-Laguerre, is provided. In this analysis, a comparison is made between these methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency in approximating solar irradiance over a specific angle range, or temperature distribution in a solar cell based on the blackbody radiation model.

In many areas of science, including computational physics, machine learning, and neural networks, it is essential to compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors. This paper introduces a novel approach called `ViViT`, which leverages deep learning to compute directional derivatives of eigenvalues efficiently. By using automatic differentiation and a novel cross-model training strategy, ViViT can improve the efficiency of computations, particularly when dealing small eigenvalues. Experimental results show that ViViT can achieve an 8x speedup in computation time compared to traditional methods, and it enables a significant reduction in energy error for stochastic gradient descent optimization, making it an effective tool for machine learning applications.

Researchers have expressed concern about bias in word embeddings generated by word2vec due to unfair treatment of words based on grammatical gender. They attempted to address this by developing methods to create gender-neutral embeddings. We find that simply averaging vector representations does not produce useful embeddings, and that word embeddings should not be assigned according to their grammatical class. Instead, our study reveals that removing gender associations with words actually improves embedding quality in Dutch, English, and French. However, the success of this method varies when applied to the language model's performance. We find that the fine-tuned BERT model's results depend on the language being used: applying a neutralization process yields better outcomes in English and French, but not in Dutch.

We derive a new technique to calculate the nilmanifold's ergodic invariant measures under given actions of SL(n,Z) where n is 2 or 3. This technique is developed from a fundamental property of character distributions in the case of compact, connected Lie groups under the action of their discrete subgroups. The key lies in the distribution's local nature. The application of this fact to the space of characters in Fuchsian groups led to the discovery of a distinct limit theorem, contrasting significantly with the dynamics of torus mappings, as highlighted in [NSY1]. Although the underlying groups in (1) are not finitely generated, their elements are distributed according to the same underlying Lie group. In contrast, the cases involving torus mappings rely on the distinct distribution of elements in the source groups.

This paper introduces a novel approach to estimating the pose of objects by utilizing low-resolution position and orientation data to improve high-resolution tracking estimates in dynamic environments, particularly when dealing with severe signal occlusions. The proposed framework integrates two modules - the flow module, which identifies and addresses the limitations of existing baseline methods, and the orientation module, which leverages low-resolution orientation data to correct high-resolution orientation estimates. By combining these modules with a coarse-to-fine strategy, we have developed an improved estimation system that outperforms existing baseline methods by an average of 3.6 degrees in total absolute error (TotalAE) across 31 datasets. The proposed method also exhibits robustness in handling severe signal occlusions, and as part of our research, we have made significant contributions in the form of new baseline algorithms, a dataset consisting of 31 estimation problems, and comprehensive comparative analyses.

In urban planning and traffic management, calculating travel time is a crucial task, and machine learning is often used for this purpose, specifically in the form of graph-based models. Our study examines gradient boosting decision trees (GBDTs) and neural networks (NNs) to compare their potential. We find that conventional GBDTs provide equally effective results as more complex graph neural networks (GNNs) but offer faster computation and easier interpretation. By utilizing GBDTs, we demonstrate how complex urban traffic patterns can be effectively modeled and highlight the feasibility of utilizing this approach within larger frameworks for land use and transport planning.

The use of cause-and-effect knowledge in causal inference models has the potential to address fairness challenges in classification tasks. New causal methods are being developed to quantify fairness non-criteria. We propose an approach to evaluate counterfactual fairness by detecting the causal effect of attributes on target variables in classification problems. We leverage a novel method that combines isotonic regression with a score-based causal inference model using score-shot learning. The approach focuses on estimating score-shot learning without needing to directly model complex target variable distributions. Our proposed approach also facilitates automatic discovery of score-shot learning causes and fairness verification. Additionally, we incorporate this algorithm into the FATE framework for classification problems. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through synthetic data experiments and image classification tasks.

The vast amounts of data generated by large radio telescopes like the LOFAR cannot be effectively handled by traditional central processing methods. To address this, a novel, fully distributed processing framework is introduced, in which each antenna independently processes its data, and a central server oversees the entire process. This framework can be adapted to an existing LOFAR software foundation and achieves a significant performance enhancement, surpassing the conventional approach by 20% in both CPU usage and disk access times.

A cutting-edge field, metaphotonics, is rapidly gaining momentum with its focus on optically triggering electron excitations through magnetic modes. The concept involves using optically triggered electric and magnetic resonances in metaatoms to examine both magnetic and magnetic-junction band structures. To investigate magnetic resonances in electron trajectories, our work involves simulating the optical response of a nanodisk array on a magnetic substrate. The simulated results, however, contradict the initial expectations. The magnetic resonance formed upon optically inducing resonances in both magnetic and electric modes was found to be more complex than anticipated. Specifically, we discovered that magnetic and electric dipole interactions generate magnetic dipole moments that are in phase and opposed. This phenomenon reveals new possibilities in magnetic metamaterials, controlled by optically induced resonances.

The effectiveness of using a movie's cast to forecast its earnings has long been acknowledged.
Previous research into a movie's "pull" - its attractiveness to viewers and associated with its release performance and box office results - has been extensive.
This study introduces innovative techniques to analyze different aspects of "pull" - a movie's "star power" - including: distribution of release dates, ticket sales, and review scores across various market sizes.
Through analysis of 24,414 movies between 2003 and 2021, several aspects of star "pull" were identified.
The results indicate that a movie's "star power" can be predicted in advance, in contrast to release-time factors like distribution patterns.
Using an unstructured model, the study estimates a movie "pull" score based on its cast and provides access to the model to allow users to evaluate any cast's potential.

Utilizing a quasi-static model, particularly one rooted in algebraic theory, we investigate the mathematical modeling and analysis of second and third-level frequency regulation. Focusing on stability issues, we illustrate how this type of regulation can significantly influence both transient stability and practical operational limits of electric networks. Our findings indicate that even with simpler, static models governing generator voltage, there exists a relationship between secondary frequency control and voltage fluctuations. Moreover, primary frequency regulation is shown to create instability-related obstacles. When controlling system frequency through the injection of active power via multiple control agents networked in sequence, we demonstrate the creation of intricate feedback loops involving both active and reactive power flows, as well as the determination of critical stability thresholds.

Cyber-physical systems encompass a broad range of physical systems influenced by various layers of software, which interacts with the system's connections and inherent properties, ultimately giving rise to connected natural-physical-cyber systems. Within the context of these systems a distinction is made between two fundamental aspects: the connectionist approach, which concentrates on the behaviour of systems with altered physical properties through control, and the informational approach, which examines the behaviour of systems influenced by connections and environments through planning. A unified framework of assumptions and nomenclature that accommodates both aspects can serve as the foundation for further analysis and research in this area, with this paper aiming to contribute through the presentation of such a framework and an extensive list of corresponding literature that classifies research endeavors within the framework and classifies various research endeavors within the framework.

Measuring the polarization of blazar UV/X-ray emissions can unlock their intrinsic properties, which are obscured by their proximity to supermassive black holes. To investigate the polarization of UV/X-ray emissions from blazars, we employed a cross-correlation technique using data from the UVIT telescope and the eROSITA X-ray telescope. Our analysis focused on a sample of ten bright blazars observed during a long-term survey, where we combined 100 seconds of UVIT data in four energy bands with 100 ms to 1 second in soft X-ray XMM-RGPSXS observations. To mitigate the influence of instrumental stray light, we selected blazars with high X-ray to UV flux ratios. Despite applying novel image reconstruction techniques and rotating the images to the celestial meridian plane, our polarization measurements were still significantly affected by stray light. To this end, we established a method to derive polarization fraction and angle from correlation coefficients, effectively removing instrumental polarization contamination. Our results showed no detectable polarization for seven blazars within the given sensitivity limits of 4.5% and 7.1% for fractions and angles, respectively. In contrast, our analysis suggested that BL Lacertae and Mrk 421 could exhibit low-level polarization consistent with systematic uncertainties.

Research has shown that how replicas are grouped together in a simulation's solutions significantly impacts the matrices describing the solutions' curvature. Specifically, simulations with certain grouping structures reach their minimum points faster than others. The difference between simulations with one-step and advanced grouping structures results in a noticeable difference in how fast the simulation reaches its minimum points. The difference between these simulation types affects the curvature of the minimum points, resulting in matrices with distinct characteristics, which can in turn affect the performance of the one-step structure in comparison to more advanced simulation structures. The distinct curvature can even lead to the one-step structure performing better than more advanced simulation structures in certain instances. The distinct curvature is linked to current research suggesting that more advanced simulation structures may not improve the performance of the optimization algorithm in the short term.

In our research, we've developed faster methods to calculate the overlap between two high-dimensional spherical objects defined by constraints on the number of dimensions and an online scheme's performance, specifically when the dimensions are recorded as integers. These algorithms utilize pre-computed tables to achieve this improvement, outperforming existing schemes by yielding larger constant values. Our work has also demonstrated that these algorithms are particularly effective when dealing with a particular type of constraint. In contrast to a recent scheme's performance on an analogous problem, our findings reveal differing results in the regime of a particular constant's value and when another type of constraint is applied, indicating a potential discrepancy in the methodologies used.

The masses derived from the light meson spectrum serve as a fundamental input to establish light quark masses, which in turn enable the calculation of the QCD sum rules for the sums of mass differences among the masses of the light baryons. This method is first demonstrated to determine the up and down quark masses through the application to the mass spectrum of the light baryons comprising the nucleon, the $\Lambda$, and the $\Sigma$. Subsequently, the mass spectrum of the nucleon, $\mathit{N}$, $\it{\Lambda}$, and $\it{\Sigma}$ baryons, as well as that of the baryon decuplet, is modelled using these values. Here, we extend the method to derive the masses of baryons involving the charm quark, as well as the quark masses for the light flavors, $\it{u}$, $\it{d}$, $\it{s}$, $\it{c}$, as well as the heavy bottom quark, $\it{b}$. Here, the chiral symmetry mass formula is utilized to model the masses of the baryons comprising the charm and bottom quarks.

Models of the sun's large-scale meridional flow have been difficult to verify due to a lack of conclusive observational evidence. To address this challenge, researchers employed the acoustic tomography technique, utilizing time delays from acoustic waves as they travel along the surface of the sun. This led to the discovery of significant horizontal flows that contradict the predicted patterns of the sun's meridional circulation. Specifically, for medium-amplitude acoustic signals, the measured flow speeds were notably higher than what was expected, ranging from 100 to 300 meters per second. The results were consistent when measured at different depths within the sun, but the speed of the horizontal flows decreased as amplitude of the acoustic signals increased. To gain further insight into the phenomena, researchers isolated the contributions of individual acoustic modes and found that specific modes were associated with the detected horizontal flows, suggesting they may be a persistent feature of the sun's atmosphere.

The magnetic field in the early universe influences both electromagnetic waves and gravitational waves in unique ways, which can be harnessed to enhance detection capabilities and test theoretical predictions. This exceptional environment not only allows for the distinction between longitudinal and transverse polarization modes of electromagnetic waves, but also offers a way to distinguish between gravitational waves polarized in parallel and anti-parallel directions to the magnetic field. This property could lead to the development of multiple detectors with overlapping sensitivities, thereby increasing the chances of detecting gravitational waves. In addition, magnetic fields can also cause electromagnetic phenomena, such as photon splitting, scattering, and polarization conversion, that may further inform our understanding of properties such as photon mass. This review explores these phenomena in the context of early universe physics.

The 4D light field (LF) image, a technology capturing scene color and direction, has the potential to revolutionize virtual reality and augmented reality. However, its application is currently hindered by computational limitations and storage limitations. Traditional compression methods, focusing solely on image quality and pixel resolution, are ineffective in meeting current requirements. A disparity-aided model is presented to address these limitations by considering the optical properties of LF images, including inter-image disparities. By estimating inter-image offsets and applying geometric transformations to align corresponding sub-images, lower resolution and higher quality can be achieved, thus significantly reducing the data storage burden. Experimental results demonstrate that this novel approach outperforms conventional LF compression methods, even under reduced resolution and higher distortion, while adhering to realistic quality metrics. Notably, this new disparity-aided model enables efficient compression of LF images, making them suitable for real-world applications.

We address the challenge of cross-lingual information retrieval (CLIR) in which a user's query is provided in a different language than the documents in the database. Most CLIR approaches rely on a single-pass model, where the user's query is matched with database contents only once. In this paper, we propose CLINE, a novel semi-interactive CLIR framework that leverages an iterative language translation process to improve retrieval accuracy. Given the user's query, CLINE alternates between translating the query and the retrieved document snippets in an alternating manner, effectively allowing the query to adapt to the user's language and vice versa. We evaluate CLINE's performance on two real-world datasets, Facebook CLIR and WSCOIR, and compare it to the state-of-the-art CLIR models. The results demonstrate CLINE's superior performance, achieving significant improvements in retrieval accuracy, recall, and user satisfaction compared to the current CLIR models. Specifically, CLINE outperforms the state-of-the-art CLIR models by a significant margin in terms of retrieval accuracy (12.5% and 14.3% improvements in pairwise matching scores), recall (17.1% and 14.1% improvements in cross-lingual matching rates), and user satisfaction (10.1% and 12.3% improvements in overall CLINE framework performance metrics).

This research presents a novel approach to demography that utilizes the principles of spatial statistics for analyzing data with detailed geographic resolution. Our demographic spatial model, inspired by the spatial multiplicative decomposition technique, breaks down complex phenomena into distinct components representing trends, spatial patterns, and random fluctuations. Utilizing comprehensive population and demographic data collected from the United States between 2000 and 2017, we apply our spatial model to analyze the trends and variations observed in the US, and compare our findings against high-resolution grid-based datasets obtained from the Google Population Services API over the course of one week. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating spatial models can reveal significant insights into the United States' demographic patterns, and that utilizing Google's high-resolution data provides a more accurate understanding of these complex phenomena. Furthermore, our study highlights the importance of considering unique spatial and temporal characteristics when analyzing the United States' demographic data.

This research introduces the concept of quantum memory betting, a quantum framework that integrates gambling, information theory, and quantum information, building upon a classical counterpart proposed by the senior author's earlier paper, with an emphasis on addressing key characteristics and their implications. The complex structure of quantum memory betting is crucial in distinguishing it from its classical counterpart. The analysis provides comprehensive insights into this novel concept, with quantum memory serving as free information, and the comparison of strategies employed by classical and quantum gamblers being a central theme of the investigation. The investigation reveals that quantum gamblers can leverage free information, encoded in quantum memory, for significant returns by applying a non-classical gambling strategy, with a maximal one-shot return equivalent to the coherent correlation between input and output random variables. However, attempting to replicate this correlation-building process may result in information loss. The initial paper introduced the fundamental model and an alternative approach for gambling with a coin toss. The current analysis explores the optimal gambling strategy, combining elements of the classical model's characteristics, and provides an essential general theorem. The analysis also delves into quantum correlations' impact on gambling returns, as well as scenarios where access to free information, encoded in quantum memory, is limited. The investigation reveals that although the initial gain factor is unbounded, repeated application of the optimal gambling strategy results in return convergence. The study utilizes various quantum frameworks, including POVMs, quantum channels, and quantum states, in conjunction with classical models. The analysis also considers the interplay between information

To assess the accuracy of bound states for anions in low-dimensional materials, we compared quasiparticle energies calculated using efficient Green's function methods with those calculated using more precise but computationally intensive gravity theory and a method based on the QED effective field theory. The results indicate that the efficiency of Green's function methods can be significantly improved without sacrificing accuracy, making them a more viable option for large anion-based low-dimensional material systems.

The Augmented BFGS algorithm is used in the analysis of data collected from the Belle II detector, corresponding to an integrated luminosity of 190 fb^-1 in the $\pi^+ \pi^- \pi^0$ decay channel to find $\Sigma^+ \to p \pi^0$ candidates, with the goal of determining the branching fraction. Results from a search in the $\Sigma^+ \to p \gamma$ decay mode are also presented to provide complementary evidence. Results from both measurement modes are consistent. The observation of decays to $\Sigma^+ \to p \pi^0$ mode is found to confirm previous studies with a 6.1 sigma significance and a branching fraction of $(1.04 \pm 0.19 \pm 0.18 ) \times 10^{-4}$.

The traditional understanding of turbulent motion in protoplanetary disks, primarily driven by the accretion process, has revealed a contrasting pattern: whereas the mid-plane exhibits a relatively calm environment, the upper layers are characterized by intense turbulence. This conventional perspective, however, fails to account for a unique form of turbulence that may coexist within the disk's mid-plane, arising from vertical gradients in the magnetic field. Our investigation builds upon this premise by utilizing particle-in-cell and particle-mesh simulations to analyze the effects of ion-cyclotron and Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities and their implications for the disk's structure and behavior. Our model suggests that vertical turbulence in the disk induces the growth of ionizing particles, thereby modifying the distribution of volatile elements such as CO and CO$_2$. Our observations indicate that a specific region within the disk's mid-plane may emit X-rays due to the presence of highly ionized particles, whereas the outer disk's molecular emissions may be affected by the ionization-driven alteration of the volatile elements' distribution.

We've developed innovative methods to remove the effects of atmospheric dispersion in ADC designs, incorporating a model that accounts for its frequency-dependent nature. Our research identifies two atmospheric dispersion models, a quadratic and an arithmetic one, and demonstrates their differences across the visible light spectrum. To improve accuracy, our model makes use of two keys: refraction constant and temperature. However, to avoid incorrect ADC calculations in the blue end of the spectrum, the arithmetic model should be avoided. To calculate the recommended quadratic model, our algorithm uses three key parameters: output image size, ADC key pair, and temperature value. Our approach offers better performance compared to existing solutions in terms of speed and accuracy, with an average error of 0.00000003 pixels in the tests.

This research demonstrates that a Bayesian neural network incorporating a Horseshoe prior can effectively address variable selection and improve predictions. The prior facilitates the identification of input variable relationships and promotes efficient weighting. We demonstrate the model's ability to identify dominant variables by utilizing the Horseshoe prior. Our findings indicate that addressing uncertainty resulting from model parameter estimation is particularly crucial. Utilizing a full Bayesian approach yields the most accurate predictions. Nonetheless, the full Bayesian method has the most extensive computational demands.

Continuous logic space constructions, including those by Pelletier and Wagner, are explored in relation to abelian group duality, with specific attention to abelian groups dualities under certain conditions. It is demonstrated that every local type space corresponding to continuous logic can be associated with an abelian group dual under a specified topology. Conversely, some groups with self-dual properties under the Bohr topology, or with groups self-dual under finer topologies, can be used to generate self-dual groups under finer topologies, thereby producing self-dual type spaces.

A collaborative learning approach, known as federated learning, enables multiple organizations to train machine learning models together, without sharing their data. Despite offering privacy benefits, organizations may still harbor concerns about model performance and training costs when participating. To address these concerns, this paper proposes a new theoretical framework that integrates the principles of fairness, privacy protection, and cost efficiency. Specifically, the research develops novel metrics for fairness and model utility across multiple organizations, as well as a cost efficiency metric to evaluate the training resources used by each one. Using these metrics, the study proposes two novel optimization techniques: one ensures that each organization receives equal treatment in terms of model accuracy and bias, while the other ensures that each organization incurs the same training costs. Moreover, the research also presents novel methods for balancing model accuracy and bias in a way that benefits all organizations. By addressing these concerns, the study offers a practical solution for resolving conflicts between the interests of various organizations participating in collaborative model training.

Research into the Light Active Neutrino Dark Matter (LANM) model has gained significant momentum, driven by its ability to simultaneously explain multiple phenomena, including the existence of dark matter, the mass of the $B$ meson, a subset of baryon asymmetry, and the anomalous magnetic moment of the electron. Previous studies investigating LANM's impact on the $B_s^0 \to sZ'$ decay and future searches for the $Z'$ at particle colliders have primarily focused on their individual contributions. This study, however, examines how the $Z'$ resonance is coupled with LANM, and how their combined effects influence the determination of dark matter abundance, $Z'$ mass, and mixing angle $\theta$, as well as the outcomes of various searches in a multifaceted, two-dimensional, and parametric manner. The results obtained demonstrate considerable discrepancies from the initial estimates, thus underscoring the necessity of considering the influence of LANM on $Z'$ decays and future searches for these particles at particle colliders, particularly in the context of stringent searches for both LANM and the $Z'$ itself.

In various wireless communication applications, genetic algorithms are frequently used to solve complex, complex problems. They can be utilized in conjunction with deep unsupervised learning methods to minimize the need for explicit mathematical calculations, particularly in scenarios involving the positioning of devices, construction of intelligent reflecting surfaces, and the generation of complex modulation schemes. This work demonstrates that unsupervised learning can achieve results on par with or surpassing those of genetic algorithms, while significantly reducing the computational complexity in certain cases.

We introduce a method for assessing individual components of beta strength within specific spin and parity states, incorporating influences from nuclear structure, through the application of a set of matrices. This approach has been evaluated using two sets of experimental data on unpaired neutron states in calcium and strontium isotopes within the A = 84 and A = 104 even-even nuclei, respectively, and by considering the effects of the nuclear potential of the parent nuclei, the influence of pairing correlations, and interactions between collectivity and single-particle levels on beta strength within daughter nuclei. The results imply that various factors contribute equally to beta strength within low-lying spin and parity states, whereas one particular configuration plays a dominant role in determining beta strength within high-spin states.

We are investigating a model comprising the minimal supersymmetric standard model plus additional singlet scalars that generate masses for right-handed neutrinos through a mechanism similar to the singlet scalar in a singlet extension of the standard model, which also accounts for dark matter's relic abundance. The model's particles exhibit a substantial coupling with both the Higgs boson and right-handed neutrinos, offering an alternative framework to standard dark matter models based on gauge extensions. Moreover, we explore possible signatures of these scalar particles within supersymmetric dark matter models, such as gaugino or fermion dark matter candidates.

This paper presents a novel machine learning approach to control complex high-dimensional dynamical systems even in the absence of substantial datasets. To achieve this, we propose an algorithm that seamlessly integrates model learning, policy learning, and system simulation under a limited data constraint. Building on the foundation of reinforcement learning (RL), our learning-based control algorithm boasts equivalent policy performance, yet outperforms traditional RL methods by leveraging an auxiliary learned system model to predict future behavior and augment available data. Moreover, our method boasts flexibility in terms of black-box systems and complex dynamics, as evidenced through the successful control of a quadrotor, a high-dimensional non-linear system.

We have successfully verified the higher-spin symmetry of the Toda conformal field theories in two-dimensional space. Our approach involved explicitly checking the validity of spin-three Ward identities, using key elements of the theory's correlation functions (three-point and four-point). These findings support existing hypotheses regarding universal properties in higher-spin conformal field.

To rectify the limitations of Generative Adversarial Networks, we introduce the 'Relation Network', a novel architecture designed to facilitate communication between G1 and G2 networks. By enabling a relational dynamic, RN outperforms traditional GANs and androgenous architectures. The success of RN is attributed to its implicit discriminator, a relationship between androgenous generators. By leveraging the 'soft relation' concept, RN fosters cooperative yet highly vigilant connections between networks. The model's efficacy is showcased by its superior image quality, demonstrated through MNIST, CIFAR10, and LSUN-Church datasets.

To attain single-photon interference in twin-field quantum key distribution without relying on true single-photon sources, an innovative approach is suggested, where a new perspective is employed. Reference frames are used and any carrier phase fluctuation is considered as the global phase reference itself. Establishing this phase reference becomes feasible through two reciprocal users' local reference frames. Moreover, our method is adaptive in nature, allowing it to adapt to various losses in channel phasors and, as a result, the loss threshold can adaptively adjust.

This work utilizes the $p$-Bergman and $p$-Fock inner products to categorize Toeplitz operators on these spaces, with operators either from to into the adjoint, or mutually, being compact based on host-source interactions.

Recent object detection models struggle with objects enclosed by irregular shapes such as polygons, leading to inaccurate object localization and classification. To improve the robustness of modern object detectors, we propose using enhanced bounding boxes that have been corrected from automatically generated annotations. To facilitate this process, we developed a framework for refining bounding-box estimates based on R-CNN results, and an object detection framework that incorporates these refined annotations. Experiments on a shape recognition dataset demonstrate that our method yields more accurate detector performance. Notably, using improved bounding-box annotations increases the accuracy of detectors by approximately 1.1%.

The extensive $^{12}$CO(1-0) and $^{13}$CO(1-0) emission observed from the innermost part of the Milky Way's disk is likely affected by self-absorption. This absorption can distort the observed spectrum, potentially masking the true extent of CO emission and making it appear more compact. To further investigate the emission's characteristics, we analyzed the influence of nearby stars on the observed spectra. By examining two specific regions in the innermost 100 pc of the Galaxy, we detected significant CO emission outside the previously established boundaries. This discovery indicates that the previously established boundaries are likely a result of the suppressed or less-visible CO emission in the direction of bright sources. Additionally, our analysis revealed a potential correlation between the suppressed CO emission and the velocity structure of the gas. This correlation implies that self-absorption is a widespread phenomenon in the gas emission in the innermost galactic regions.

Transformer models, with their inductive self-attention, excel in capturing distant long-range connections but lack a inductive bias for efficient spatial representation. In contrast, convolutional networks are naturally suited for spatial representation, but struggle with distant connections. To address this, we suggest incorporating Transformer blocks as a substitution for the initial convolutional stem in conventional convolutional networks. This innovative design, termed StemTransformer, serves as a powerful framework that merges the strengths of convolutional networks and Transformers, yielding superior performance on benchmarks such as ADE20k, Cityscapes, PASCAL VOC, and MSRA-B.

A novel approach for mortality forecasting involves a two-factor model with a spatial structure, where one factor is local and both factor loadings change over time. This model can outperform the classical Cairns-Parol model in retrospective studies. To apply this model, we developed a novel transition model using Markov Chain Monte Carlo to estimate its parameters. A simulation study confirmed that incorporating time-varying loading factors leads to more accurate and stable forecasts. Additionally, we demonstrated that a separate transition model can improve forecasting accuracy. Finally, we applied and evaluated this model on US mortality data and mortality data in Spain.

A neural architecture search method named NeAR was recently proposed, using re-archival to decrease early convergence issues. However, the use of contrastive learning in NeAR led to interference from non-augmented examples, hindering its performance on the BERT corpus. This study aims to address the limitations of NeAR and mitigate performance degradation caused by early interference. To achieve this, a retrieval approach inspired by contrastive learning is explored to filter out interfering examples and enable more effective learning. The modified method, denoted as rNeAR, employs negative sample isolation to eliminate interference and demonstrate improved performance. The rNeAR method surpasses NeAR by over 10% and over 5% on the BERT corpus, outperforming the ELECTRA model with better accuracy. The relevant code has been shared on GitHub.

Time-series feature extraction is a crucial task requiring skilled training and domain knowledge, often leading to suboptimal results due to its difficulty. To address this challenge, we developed the ` theft software package offering an intuitive interface for students to perform this task seamlessly. The package overcomes the limitations of existing tools by overcoming three main obstacles: the heavy training curve, rigid structure, and overlooked feature importance. To accomplish this, the package incorporates three core components: automatic feature engineering, a time-series analysis library, and an adaptive ensemble classifier. Additionally, it allows for the extraction of important features by integrating the ` timeDate and caret packages. We also incorporated the Shapley value method to feature importance and implemented the Light Gradient Boosting Machine algorithm for superior accuracy.

Geodesic completeness is crucial to the extended definitions of hyperbolicity in CAT(0) and CAT(-1) spaces. A significant result by Bridson and Gromov establishes a connection between geodesic completeness and the CAT(0) geodesic completeness of a torus quotient. The property of geodesic completeness is then translated to algebraic terms via the properties of the fundamental group. A novel class of CAT(0) torus quotients with hyperbolic fundamental groups is discovered, challenging the long-standing conjecture that such a class does not exist. It is demonstrated that these discovered classes have no Gromov hyperbolic alternatives in CAT(0) geodesic completeness. Furthermore, CAT(0) torus quotients with hyperbolic fundamental groups containing a hyperbolic element as an axis-preserving automorphism are identified and described.

The shared task presented at NAACL 2020, involves the concepts evaluation challenge, a task that requires models to predict qualities of human translators and area specialists in their respective fields. From June to July 2019, researchers were granted access to task-specific data, including quality assessments performed by various translators and experts at a designated conference from March to June that year. In order to ensure fairness, the data was gathered by independent evaluators to prevent biased predictions, with experiments ultimately focusing on evaluating various data processing methods, including both text and knowledge graph representations. In examining these methods, we discovered that both individual translators and experts show consistency in their assessments when they are not aware of their previous concepts, with both text and knowledge graph representations yielding similar results.

We revisit and expand upon the eigenchannel theory, which explains how specific characteristics of waves interact with static environments, offering a framework to categorize complex dynamic patterns. By focusing on these fundamental patterns, the theory helps us understand their interrelation with the system's intense features, such as high-intensity light paths in coherent systems. We explore this concept with an experimental study of laser illumination through static fire scars on lunar surface, revealing distinct pathways where energy is concentrated. The majority of intensity within these paths corresponds to the system's dominant natural frequencies, known as the lowest-order eigenchannels, and deviating from this main pathway results in a decrease in intensity. Additionally, the eigenchannel theory provides a framework to predict and understand the occurrence of high-intensity features in waves, including cases with non-coherent systems, where a modified, incoherent version of the theory is also considered.

Neural networks have proven invaluable in solving complex visual problems. However, these models are prone to data leakage, making it crucial to develop methods for developing reliable algorithms. In a recent study, I investigated the effectiveness of iterative magnitude pruning as a test for visual models. Surprisingly, I discovered that it does not consistently serve as a reliable test harness, even in cases where it does not lead to significant loss in accuracy. Furthermore, I identified some methods of overpruning that do not degrade overall model performance. These findings highlight the need for more robust and reliable test harnesses for visual models.

This study delves into the psychological aspects of lotteries from a negative expected utility perspective. It demonstrates that, in most cases, lotteries do not yield positive returns unless the jackpot falls within a specific mid-range. Furthermore, a mathematical model is developed to find the optimal strategy for purchasing tickets in full lotteries to break even. Our findings reinforce the notion that state-run lotteries are a reliable way for citizens to contribute to public funds, especially when played consistently.

This study examines the application of the large-charge expansion to the $SO(N)$ model in 3-dimensional space, focusing on its utility in exploring critical phenomena. We examine the first three non-zero terms of the expansion for the critical exponent $\eta$ and $v$, and observe that these quantities align with results obtained from Monte-Carlo simulations.

Our research suggests that an unbalanced, localized strain field is required to influence valley Hall transport within honeycomb lattice models. By examining the effect of varying local strain on such systems, we discover that valence and conduction band extrema respond differently, resulting in different momentum shifts of valley K' and K. Contrary to earlier research, our findings indicate that valley Hall behavior is bandwidth-dependent, with resonance between valleys K and K' occurring when this disparity exceeds the valley gap. To illustrate this phenomenon, we demonstrate how electrical transport changes when applying local strain to warped models of graphene, WSe2, MoS2, and flat-band models like flat-band graphene and chiral models.

Contrastive learning has become a leading approach for domain-adaptive image classification without requiring labeled data in the target domain. The method typically involves extracting features using a unsupervised pre-trained model and employing another model to map these features to class predictions, with the objective of minimizing the divergence between the two models during training. Recent research indicates that the "model soup" technique, which averages the outputs of the two trained models, can significantly enhance the generalization performance of models processed in this manner. In this work, we investigate the theoretical underpinnings of model soup, demonstrating that the technique not only improves predicted accuracy but also enhances confidence in predictions. Furthermore, we identify key factors affecting the model soup efficacy and develop additional model combination methods based on these insights. The experimental results obtained on three different settings confirm the practical utility of our proposed approaches.

Recent preprints have cast doubt on the effectiveness of t-SNE, suggesting its claimed ability to preserve both local and global data structures may not hold true. We investigate the core t-SNE method, uncovering a critical flaw in its normalization approach, which fails to account for spherical data. This flaw is attributed to the use of a 2D Gaussian distribution, which does not accurately model spatial proximity on spherical data. The Gaussian distribution decreases with distance, but on a sphere, proximity should increase with distance, which only the harmonic function可以实现. We propose replacing the Gaussian with the uniformly spreading distribution, USD, and develop the uniformly spreading dimensionality reduction method, USR. We use theoretical proofs to show that USR can effectively preserve both local proximity and global data structures. We provide empirical evidence from simulations, showing that USR is robust to various data distributions, including challenging cases, such as Sierpinski's gasket data, which has been problematic for t-SNE. We also demonstrate that USR is resistant to commonly reported t-SNE failures.

Using advanced renormalization group theory, we offer a comprehensive analysis of how polaron factors evolve as interactions grow stronger through a complete set of diagrammatic calculations. Contraryingly, the self-energy determined by the Luttinger-Ward functional exhibits substantial deviations from its single particle-hole counterpart, especially at strong coupling strengths where it connects to the large-$N$ results from Shibaeva et al. [arXiv:2001.09755]. Additionally, we observe a substantial discrepancy between the Z factor obtained from the full series and its single particle-hole analogue across all interaction strengths.

The digital-analog quantum computing (DAQ) strategy combines specific types of native Hamiltonians through classically controllable pulses and applies discrete unitary operations from standard gates to efficiently simulate complex many-body systems. 

Our proposed DAQ scheme involves using a modified two-dimensional tight-binding Hamiltonian to model the continuous-time dynamics of the Fermi-Hubbard model. 

To capture various aspects of the Fermi-Hubbard model, particularly strong correlations, we combine the DAQ approach with discrete time evolution gates, creating a versatile platform for studying high-energy physics and condensed matter phenomena, including high-temperature superconductivity.

This research focuses on identifying specific matching polynomials, particularly those of complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs, using a novel approach based on their associated linear maps. The study provides evidence that every set of real numbers can form the characteristic polynomial for a specific linear map. Additionally, the work determines the mapping characteristics for the matching polynomials in question, leading to a novel method for testing matrix adjacency to these specific graphs. The findings are further extended to examine anti-isomorphism between these graphs, proving that no such relationship exists. The characterizations from this research are then generalized to other types of graphs, including those that are incomplete and bipartite, and the study explores the connection between a graph's structure and its matching polynomial.

The underlying mechanisms driving the chaotic behavior in the quantum representations are determined by how pseudo-Anosov elements act within the representations of the mapping class groups of surfaces. This is investigated by analyzing the asymptotic behavior of the traces of the closed geodesics, which is a specific type of problem known as the Tauberian problem. This is understood by breaking down the action of the mapping class on the hyperbolic surface, which is the dominant term in the Tauberian assertion and is derived from the classical results for Teichm\"uller representations. This understanding is then used to develop precise statements regarding the behavior of the twisted traces of the surface group, which is a specific type of representation associated with the surface. This is achieved by combining the underlying geometric understanding with the methods developed in the field of representation theory. This is then applied to the case of surfaces defined by triangles and a particular type of representation associated with a triangle group, which is the so-called triangle representation. This is achieved by analyzing the geometric structure associated with a triangle and its associated group theory and representation theory. This is then applied to the case of surfaces defined by Hecke triangle groups and a particular type of representation associated with a Hepp matrix, which is the so-called Hepp matrix representation. This is achieved by analyzing the geometric structure associated with a Hepp matrix, which is related to a triangle group, and the specific properties associated with the matrix, which is the so-called Hepp matrix, within the context

This study investigates how organizations utilize Scrum in the face of ongoing and significant shifts in their operational landscapes, driven by advances in technology. The research involves an in-depth examination of how these events reshape the nature of work and how organizations adapt by integrating Agile methodologies like Scrum. Furthermore, we explore the impact of such adaptations on organizational performance. A survey-based approach involving 172 respondents from 57 organizations reveals that organizations which have adopted Scrum practices, particularly when implemented on a large scale, are more likely to achieve their objectives. Interestingly, this correlation is not as pronounced for organizations that employ Scrum only in partial capacity. Ultimately, this study highlights how organizational achievements can be influenced by shifts in work dynamics and how leveraging these changes through the adoption of Agile methodologies like Scrum can contribute to success.

The number of distinct eigenvalues calculated by the characteristic polynomial of an arrowhead matrix, whose elements have the general form $a_i + b_i e^{i\theta}$, is counted by the Gau--Wu number $n + \lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1$, except in instances where $n = 2j + 1$ and $b_i = (-1)^j b$ remains constant, in which case it equals the partition number $1 + 2 + \ldots + n/2 = n/2 + 1 + 1$ multiplied by $|\theta/\pi|$. Furthermore, using the characteristic polynomial of the matrix raised to a power, we can compute the eigenvalues of the matrix when raised to the power, assuming its elements take the form $a_i + b_i e^{i\theta/m}$.

This document, the second iteration of ALICE's heavy-flavour collaboration's Performance Report, summarizes results from 2015-2018 for the p-p collision at 13 TeV and the Pb-Pb collision at 5.02 TeV in the range of transverse momentum up to 100GeV/c for the p-Tp and up to 30GeV/c for the high-energy region in the Pb-Pb. The report describes the detection of beauty and charm hadrons through the detection of their decay products in the ALICE detector, and evaluates its performance under different collision conditions. The report updates previous reports, first published in 2015 and 2017, with the following references: [AAJ915, AAJ916, AAJ917, AAJ918, AAJ919, AAJ920, AAJ921, AAJ922, AAJ923, AAJ924, AAJ925, AAJ926, AAJ927, AAJ928, AAJ929, AAJ930, AAJ931, AAJ932, AAJ933, AAJ934, AAJ935, AAJ936, AAJ937, AAJ938, AA

This paper introduces an innovative method of representing color sequences using the topological concept of connected components, which is beneficial in various fields including genetics, data mining, and computer vision. To achieve this, we employ a combination of ordered trees, the k-nearest neighbor graph, and the Minkowski distance to convert color sequences into hierarchical representations. The analysis of the k-nearest neighbor graph's persistent homology and Betti numbers across color classes generates a novel, hierarchical color map, ultimately leading to the development of an efficient algorithm that categorizes sequences based on their topological characteristics.

This study investigates power control strategies for large and complex interference networks, specifically examining the properties of binary power control, and in the process, reveals two crucial concepts - the notional interference interference interference (NII) and the notional coherence length - that simplify the description of massive interference networks. These concepts enable the construction of two power control protocols, binary power control and auto-paired power control, both of which outperform their counterparts in terms of sum-rate performance, especially under high signal-to-noise conditions, and exhibit remarkably stable performance even when the number of users varies significantly.

The extensive research conducted to establish probabilistic models has proven ineffective when applied to the auditing process due to its reliance on precise calculations. In contrast, researchers have examined the potential of using a generalized probabilistic framework based on Dempster-Shafer mass models, which can effectively demonstrate varying auditor interests in different transaction accounts. The application of this framework to time-consuming transaction accounts revealed a fine-grained probability distribution that reflects the relative importance of distinct transaction categories such as revenues, allowances, taxes, subsidies, and interest payments.

A modified Approach, called Acceptance Rejection Stitching (ARST), is presented here as a point process simulation method, combining separate algorithms that handle distinct data ranges. This method has its roots in the chaining technique initially used in the estimation of multivariate distribution functions. Through simulations, the ARST method has been shown to yield significant performance improvements over single algorithm implementations when used to simulate point processes with heavy tailed marks and large range of marks' support. It has also been demonstrated that each step in the ARST approach can be parallelized, thus facilitating efficient computation.
