In this work, we investigate galilean transformations influenced by Generalized Uncertainty Principle (GUP), treating the most general form of GUV as an effective GUP linear function of momentum. Through this approach, deformed galilean transformations yield the same mass conservation law as Lorentz transformations under General Relativity theory's framework. Comparing energy conservation in quantum mechanics as it relates to GUP with energy conservation in classical mechanics as it relates to galilean transformations, a consistent energy conservation law is found that aligns with the classical case.

In task scheduling for multitasking systems, processing tasks are assigned to tasks that request it and can be preempted as needed. Previous work on dependent task scheduling has focused on how to effectively use shared processing capacity. However, current studies have not simultaneously optimized both the task allocation and scheduling decisions. While existing work has demonstrated efficient use of shared capacity, some results show that even with infinite processing efficiency, tasks may still fail to complete on time, implying that current methods do not guarantee meeting deadlines for tasks even in the most efficient scenarios. To address this gap, our paper proposes a new objective function that minimizes scheduling delays and then develops an efficient approach for dynamically allocating processing capacity in real-time. Building upon this foundation, we present several optimal policy algorithms capable of ensuring timely task completion when optimal scheduling is feasible. Furthermore, a non-preemptive algorithm is proposed, ensuring that tasks will not exceed their scheduling constraints for tasks of a certain type.

This study investigates various aspects of controlled robotic hopping on soft ground. We employ simplified linearized models to determine optimal strategies for pre-imposed impulses on varying surfaces, such as soft ground and compliant walls. Furthermore, we explore the effectiveness of feedback mechanisms in maintaining consistent hopping phases and accurately tracking complex, non-circular trajectories. The exceptional performance of these control strategies is demonstrated through high-fidelity simulations of a single-link robot with a soft ground and compliant floor, thereby offering potential solutions to similar challenges in legged locomotion and actuated systems.

We propose an innovative approach to rapidly and efficiently update large-scale IoT networks by utilizing simultaneous transmissions (CT). Our solution addresses the challenge of firmware Over-The-Air updates in IoT deployments by increasing scalability and reliability. As an alternative to traditional store-and-forward routing protocols, our approach leverages CT to minimize scalability and transmission issues. However, due to IoT devices' hardware limitations, our method involves the uplink transmission of firmware by base stations, which introduces new challenges such as signal interference and power management. We present a CT-based firmware update protocol that maximizes CT benefits while ensuring minimal signal distortion through uplink power control and transmission scheduling. Our proposed solution utilizes CT to facilitate rapid dissemination of data within IoT networks, increasing robustness and transmission efficiency. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations using a real-world CT system, showing significant improvements in uplink transmission times and success rates compared to conventional CT-based protocols.

A novel method called thermally-assisted inverse localization is proposed to investigate the transition from thermal states to many-body localization. The method involves calculating the fractal dimension related to the self-energy in the basis of eigenstates of the Hamiltonian. Through the application of a variable-temperature version of the density-matrix renormalization group band structure method, we studied the thermal to many-body localization transition in the 1D spin-1 Heisenberg chain with dipole-dipole interactions. The fractal dimension at the ground state was also examined. We found that the fractal dimension changes depending on whether the system is in a thermal state or many-body localized, nearly constant in both cases. Additionally, we identified a temperature where the fractal dimension has a local maximum as the system transitions from a temperature where it behaves like a black hole to being localized. We have further investigated the validity of this approach in relation to level spacing statistics and explored its potential to study other models in the future.

A new algorithm, 'kBM-DP+', was created to solve the MultipleTargets problem, which involves finding the shortest path between k specified points on a grid with an obstacle, by integrating 'foldamers' into the search process and adjusting efficiency by reducing the grid's dimensions. Compared to traditional approaches, this algorithm significantly speeds up computation while yielding paths of similar quality; for instance, on an 8x8 grid 5 times faster, on a 16x16 grid 9 times faster, on a 32x32 grid 26 times faster, and so on. Furthermore, this algorithm was used to investigate how peptides bind to α-helical structures, and in doing so discovered new structures and validated existing predictions.

Inspired by the widespread issue of deep convolutional neural networks' vulnerability to adversarial examples, researchers investigated whether similar problems exist in a quantum classifier. An experiment involving the same MNIST dataset was conducted, but using f-QLearning with the Varying QAOA QAOA5 Hamiltonian on the IBMQ Quantum Service. Additionally, the study involved creating adversarial examples using the L1, L2, and Linfinity methods, which were then analyzed to be classified by the quantum classifier. It was found that most adversarial examples were incorrectly categorized by the quantum classifier, but some were accurately identified. Furthermore, although most of the adversarial examples were misclassified, some non-adversarial examples from the MNIST dataset were also misclassified. These findings suggest that further research is needed to be conducted regarding quantum machine learning and adversarial examples.

The domain S^1 on a given domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb R^2$ plays a significant role in determining the optimal Steklov eigenvalues, particularly in investigating whether a given domain $\overline\Omega$ offers a lower or upper bound for the volume-normalized $l$-th Steklov eigenvalue $\sigma^2_l(\overline\Omega, \volume(\overline\Omega))$. Previous research has demonstrated that for non-circular domains $\Omega$, a circular domain $\mathbb D$ yields the upper bound $\sigma^2_l(\mathbb D, \volume(\mathbb D))$ under specific conditions, namely if $l$ is a perfect square. In contrast, a new lower bound has been established by considering a hexagonal domain $\Hex$ as $\sigma^2_l(\Hex, \volume(\Hex,))$, applying to the case when $l$ does not meet the required congruence condition.

Recent studies showcasing process execution alignments have shown significant potential in exploring and explaining process behavior deviations from various models. Current research demonstrates the efficacy of infix and postfix alignments in pinpointing deviations from models represented as Petri nets or high-level process nets respectively, providing novel possibilities for application in process execution analysis. Although the individual merits of each method are well-established, a need arises to systematically apply both alignments to the same model-class pair in order to fully comprehend their distinct capabilities and limitations. Researchers have recently proposed hybrid alignments, which integrate both infix and postfix components to represent executions of Petri net models. Despite their potential to provide improved explanatory power over the sole application of either alignment type, several challenges hinder the practical utility of hybrid alignments, primarily stemming from excessive flexibility in the hybrid composition. A novel hybrid alignment known as l-hybrid alignments has been introduced to counterbalance this flexibility, however it comes with significant demands that significantly limit its applicability. This research introduces a novel l-hybrid alignment variant for Petri net models, specifically bifurcating models, leveraging the inherent structure to reduce demands and provide meaningful explanations. The proposed l-l-hybrid alignment is proven to be a special case of l-hybrid alignments, with notable experimental findings indicating its superior performance over the corresponding l-hybrid alignment variant.

This paper introduces the use of deep neural networks to enhance the accuracy of radio propagation models based on geometry, addressing the limitations of conventional algorithms. The effectiveness of deep convolutional neural networks is examined in the context of predicting signal strength, taking into account building heights as the primary factor influencing propagation conditions. The proposed method leverages 3D 1D convolution operations to identify patterns in building height distributions along the transmission path and incorporates an additive noise layer to simulate variability in real-world signals. The results demonstrate that trained models can accurately predict measured signal strengths, offering a practical solution for real-time prediction with minimal computational requirements.

This study introduces a novel method for integrating validation algorithms into the Temporal Planning Framework. Through this composition, we develop TEA VPerF, a temporal planning system that utilizes the Yices 1.2 solver and incorporating checks from the PyOPED validator. Our results, which we verified in a testing environment of over 1000 LTL problems from the MEX benchmark, demonstrate that verifying TEA VPerF's solutions enhances both the speed and solution quality by eliminating infeasible options and reassigning priorities to improve solution findings.

This study examines the misallocation of generation capacities due to model limitations in long-term power system planning. The primary objective is to determine the extent of these errors and identify ways to minimize them. To achieve this, we evaluate multiple models with varying temporal and spatial resolutions and compare the results with the optimal model that overcomes all constraints. Our findings indicate the following: (1) The most significant impacts result from underrepresenting temporal resolution, with costs up to 33% higher than the optimal model. The extent of this overinvestment disparity depends on local storage costs and the specific technology profiles at hand. (2) Spatial resolution issues are far less pronounced, contributing only about 1% to additional costs relative to underrepresenting temporal resolution. (3) Both types of errors can become self-correcting if higher-resolution model outcomes are utilized as initial conditions in lower-resolution models, thereby mitig the risks of under- or overinvestment.

Recent work on Vlasov-Poisson models involving fluid boundaries has inspired similar work on the dynamics of charged particle ensembles near ionized metal boundaries. This involves exploring the large-time behaviors of the neutral Vlasov-Poisson model with various boundary conditions and the semi-neutral ionic Vlasov-Poisson model with a modified Poisson equation boundary condition. These investigations led to the discovery of a generalized fluid model that accurately captures the long-term dynamics of the system.

This study aims to identify the appropriate search terms for tasks involving changes in software.
As part of this endeavor, a adaptation-then-combine strategy is implemented via a
reverse adaptation, during which the standard TextRank and POSRank algorithms are modified.
A total of 122 adaptations are utilized to fine-tune these initial rankings by integrating
newly defined features derived from associated text.
Our approach combines the initially ranked terms with those established by the features.
A comprehensive evaluation using various search engines has assessed the effectiveness of our
methodology in identifying suitable search terms on a larger scale.
Results indicate that our approach outperforms the baseline rankings achieved by TextRank
and POSRank in 80% of cases, with precision rates of 10%, 20%, and 30% respectively.

The behavior of ultrasound in gel-like substances originating from iron-oxide nanofibers under varying frequencies, durations and thresholds of high-intensity signals has been investigated. It was discovered that the pattern in which gel particles move when exposed to high-intensity signals varies greatly and depends on multiple factors such as signal strength and duration. By comparing observed movement patterns with the resulting gel properties, researchers were able to define a new type of gel that reacts to high-intensity signals and exhibits unique gel-like qualities. Specifically, as the level of high-intensity signals increases, the gel's particles become less dense and more elastic. Conversely, the physical properties of the gel's particles, such as size and concentration, do not significantly affect the gel's behavior. Ultimately, this study provides a novel understanding of gel behavior that is unique to certain types of materials made from iron-oxide nanofibers.

To prove the Collatz conjecture, we will employ mathematical induction, starting by redefining the terms "even" and "odd" in the context of the natural numbers, N. We will then outline a plan to demonstrate the validity of the conjecture for all positive integers, N.

In document classification, we use visual highlights to aid humans in understanding machine learning decisions, leveraging explainable AI techniques. 
However, current methods fall short in visually presenting explanations to users, limiting their utility and thus our research aims to bridge this gap. 
To address this challenge, we have developed a novel approach to generate unified predictions and visualizations simultaneously, leveraging both text and spatial knowledge. 
We employ both global and local interpretation strategies incorporating our method, evaluating it on diverse datasets and comparing it to established baselines. 
The results demonstrate that the integration of box-sparse and column-sparse attention mechanisms significantly enhances the accuracy of our approach, thereby outperforming the baselines in underscoring text regions vital for document classification.

We have modified the Gale-Shapley and deferred acceptance algorithms to incorporate public reputation ratings in large markets, and our research explores the impact of these ratings on algorithmic utility outcomes. Our study assumes GP preferences with a continuous range, and the public rating system is designed to account for the true types of each agent, representing their expected algorithmic gain due to rating increases or decreases under these modified algorithms. The results show that there exists a threshold $\bar{\gamma}$ for concavity of the rating impact functions such that, if the average rating in society exceeds this threshold, the modified algorithms lead to either the men-optimal or women-optimal matchings. The threshold $\bar{\gamma}$ effectively classifies the impact function's behavior based on rating levels.

Automated scoring of summarization outputs is a complex challenge.
In this paper, we develop a novel approach that uses neural networks to
evaluate the quality of summaries using QRSQ, a comprehensive metric that
surpasses existing methods by increasing correlation with human scoring from
0.34 to 0.55 on the CNN/DailyMail dataset, achieving a maximum score diversity
of 0.62, and extending application beyond the 11-13 CG11-13 datasets.
Additionally, we demonstrate the flexibility of QRSQ by applying it to
summarization tasks in Q&A, scientific Q&A, machine translation, and image
captioning.

This research introduces a novel sensor fusion approach called BEVFusion, utilizing the Transformer architecture to utilize information from cameras and LiDAR in object detection tasks within autonomous vehicles. By leveraging these sensors in this specific framework, it has been demonstrated that BEVFusion outperforms previous techniques, having LiDAR failures negatively impacting performance by approximately 2.5 mAP, while camera errors do so by around 2.2 mAP. Furthermore, when simulating LiDAR malfunctions, the model surpassed the performance of previous methods by 1.12 mAP, camera errors were surpassed by 1.02 mAP, and achieved higher accuracy when both sensors failed, surpassing the previous methods by 2.5 mAP. It also features enhanced interpretability by effectively handling missing sensor data due to its capability to utilize camera images in object detection tasks.

We introduce a universal fluctuating hydrodynamics framework that takes into account the fluctuating hydrodynamics (FH) and its spatial and temporal dynamics, encompassing interface phenomena, and its interactions with the surrounding bulk media. To validate our approach, we first apply it to the highly nonlinear Navier-Stokes equation, and its turbulent state at high Reynolds numbers. By analyzing turbulent flows in three-dimensional space, FH equation offers a quantifiable measure of turbulence energy dissipation that is consistent with physical principles and past research. FH results are then compared to the deterministic Navier-Stokes equation, which offers only a qualitative understanding of dissipation. Furthermore, FH results are verified by simulating the turbulent flow and calculating the statistical correlation between temperature fluctuations and dissipation rates, which shows consistency with direct numerical simulations of turbulent flows. Next, we discuss the applicability of the FH equation to other nonlinear PDEs and its relationships with stochastic PDEs in mathematical literature, which we analyze in terms of spatial and temporal dynamics. Finally, we explore the implications of the proposed framework for the physical understanding of fluid dynamics and other fields of physics.

We've conducted an experiment where a diffraction-strengthened laser,, interacts with a fluid heated by a separate CO2 laser, resulting in enhanced diffraction of the interaction light in the liquid. As we vary the CO2 laser, we see periodic changes in the diffraction pattern, including in-phase and out-of-phase coherences, fluid motion, and fluid boiling.

The design repository growing at an increasingly rapid pace has fueled research in Design Mining, a subfield of Computer-Aided Design. A promising direction within this subfield is uncovering design conclusions from available resources to augment a designer's knowledge. Although current approaches uncovering these conclusions have made progress, they still suffer from instability in their results and lack of adaptability across different projects. To address these issues, we present an approach that examines multitude of aggregate design conclusions at a time, searching for those with consistent patterns across numerous unrelated design projects, and applying this to a real-world test involving multiple project comparisons. Our proposed method is found to enhance the reliability of our conclusions and is applicable to a wider range of comparison scenarios. A replicate study conducted in a real-world setting shows that this technique effectively filters out inconclusive and irrelevant research findings.

The proliferation of IoT devices has led to a significant increase in data generation, posing significant processing challenges for both classical data streams and data streams with spatial components (GeoStreams). In response, existing data stream processing systems struggle to cope with the rapid pace and vast amounts of data being generated by IoT devices. Tackling these issues, we introduce H-STREAM, a high-performance, stream-processing framework specifically designed for IoT devices, which has been developed to overcome associated speed and volume hurdles. By leveraging in-place processing and multi-level indexing, H-STREAM effectively handles spatio-temporal data streams while maintaining a low processing latency. Leveraging modern storage technologies and parallel architectures, H-STREAM efficiently processes data streams with varying levels of spatial and temporal indexing, offering users a flexible and flexible framework for data analysis and processing. Our experimental results demonstrate H-STREAM's capability to process high-volume data streams with low processing latency and excellent scalability.

Our study compares two methods for calculating the cross-section for vector-like quark pair production at hadron colliders. Firstly, we evaluate the resilience of a resonant signal model, which assumes independent vector-like quark decays in the presence of off-shell effects and interference. Secondly, we investigate the effect of non-resonant diagrams on top of resonant ones, which can bias the cross-section estimation. A study on the topological characteristics of vector-like quark events reveals how these non-resonant diagrams influence the observed signal and cross-section. Our results demonstrate that in the case of certain vector-like quark masses and decay rates, these non-resonant diagrams significantly impact the observables, resulting in a different cross-section comparison with the standard model. This understanding is crucial for the design of future collider programs.

This research contributes to the growth of SPARQL query generation from natural language. A pre-trained Transformer-based model is utilized to translate natural language questions into SPARQL queries. Several enhancements to this model are made, including the incorporation of additional training data from OWLLite, a contextual wrapper for generated queries, and a copy mechanism to efficiently handle long-tail entities. The incorporation of these improvements showcases superior performance over prior models, particularly when generating queries for less common entities. Extensive experiments validate these findings.

Recent advancements in link-based field detection methods have successfully identified numerous computer science research fields, but their effectiveness is hindered by their inability to account for the research settings in which individual studies are published. By accessing the publication venues associated with each study, it becomes possible to track the geographical and institutional developments of computer science research over time, thus offering a more comprehensive understanding of the system's evolution and field detection capabilities.

This research addresses contemporary challenges in formally verifying the resilience of deep neural networks, particularly for control applications like those in vision-based robotic systems. By leveraging mutual learning, recently popularized in computer vision and machine learning communities, we develop new approaches to verifying deep neural networks under adversarial conditions. MUTL, the proposed method, leverages the concept of mutual adversarial examples, widely studied in machine learning, to create specialized tools that extend Levenberg-Marquardt learning algorithms specifically designed for verifying neural networks in control applications. MUTL leverages the synergy between Levenberg-Marquardt and mutual adversarial examples, enabling precise evaluation of deep neural network resilience. MUTL builds upon previous research involving Levenberg-Marquardt and adversarial examples, initially applied to verifying single-input single-output robotic systems, and now extends its application to verifying multi-input multi-output robotic systems, thus expanding its scope and utility.

Functorial clustering schemes are utilized to address inconsistent results in clustering. They serve as a means to attach functors to clustering algorithms, which link objects and coobjects to cones of varying homality. Recent studies introduced a framework for analyzing clustering in single-linkage clusters, which usually suffer from structure loss. Our study extends this scheme to mitigate structure loss, which occurs when partitioning based on cluster merging. We apply this to the 'Algebraic Length' functor, which is used to address cluster splitting issues in single-linkage clusters.

Recent advancements in tensor completion and its applications in video processing, such as compression, imaging, and TDI, have been significant. However, most existing algorithms based on tensor completion don't account for motion in video data, which can severely impact their performance under dynamic conditions. This study presents a novel approach, where a video editing problem is first formulated using low-rank tensor properties before transitioning to an optimization-focused perspective suitable for algorithmic implementation. The proposed method capitalizes on the R3Net optimization network, showcasing high efficiency in both static and motion-filled video editing tasks, particularly in achieving better results compared to competing methods. Experimental results also indicate that the introduced method is adaptable to various low-rank tensor-based applications.
A comprehensive classification of the infinite-dimensional Nichols algebras associated with classical Weyl groups has been achieved, given their braiding matrix with diagonal entries of -1.

Within rotating waves, we investigated the formation of inertial wave turbulence and its corollary, the verification of the $E^{- rac{3}{2}}$ spectrum first theorized by Goldstein. An equivalent, distinct turbulent regime can be observed when the rotation is weak, resulting in the verification of the Stewartson-McWilliams spectrum derived by McWilliams. The study employed anisotropic superfluids as a test case due to their capability to mimic the inertial wave, thanks to effective mass terms and effective plasma frequencies generated by superconducting d-waves, thus circumventing the constraints of the Landau critical velocity. The turbulent flow was simulated numerically in superconducting circuits composed of two coupled transmission lines, emulating the experimental setup. The results confirmed the $E^{- rac{3}{2}}$ and $E^{-2}$ spectra, providing robust validation of the underlying theoretical models.

We introduce IGLN, a novel normalization technique that modifies a graph over time to solve the Maximum Weight Independent Set problem in near-linear time for graphs with sparsity conditions when the given parameter k is a constant. Our normalization technique, inspired by iterative graph normalization, has also been applied to other optimization problems such as multicut and other applications of the independent set problem. The first application of graph normalization to the maximum weight independent set problem has made it possible to achieve an algorithm running in time O*(2ck) with a bounded pre-processing step. The performance can be replicated by first applying a bounded sparsity condition to the graph with S(c) nodes and then using the known algorithm to find the maximum weight independent set. Our approach also has the added benefit of being able to certify the optimality of the solution obtained by only analyzing the normalized graph and its remaining non-constant fraction of the original graph. Our results further allow us to improve the existing algorithms for the maximum weight independent set by reducing the optimization step from O*(nk^3) to a bound dependent on the given graph's parameter κ(S,c) and the bound N(κ(S), W(S)), with the bound depending on the given graph's sparsity conditions. Our algorithm's ability to certify the solution obtained by only analyzing the normalized graph has also allowed us to replicate the algorithm's performance in the case of unweighted graphs with a bound O*(2ck) with a bound dependent on the given graph's parameter κ(S

We've performed numerical studies of the Landau Level (LL) oscillations in graphene when it's subjected to both an electric field perpendicular to its plane and a magnetic field. When the electric field is applied in the form of an out-of-plane EAM, it induces two-band LL oscillations, and when combined with a perpendicular magnetic field, it also generates 3D LL oscillations. In our analysis, we broke down the out-of-plane EAM into its Fourier components in the z-direction, allowing us to identify which components resonate with the magnetic field and give rise to the observed 3D LL oscillations, which in turn influence the 2-band LL oscillations. Furthermore, our investigation revealed that when the magnetic field is altered, additional resonance conditions emerge due to sideband components in the Fourier decomposition, resulting in new LL oscillations and affecting the 2-band LL oscillations.

We have conducted a radio observation of the M dwarf binary CR Draconis using the MWA in June 2020, revealing intriguing non-thermal emission. The emission, detected at levels up to 6 mJy between 70-260 MHz, shares similarities with galactic wind emission observed in Jupiter, while also exhibiting unique characteristics. Notably, the emission is less intense at lower frequencies than in Jupiter, displays structure-dependent polarization, and predominantly polarized in a mode perpendicular to the plane of the system. Based on our findings, we propose a model for CR Draconis that explains its radio emission. The M dwarf component of the system likely produces gyrosynchrotron emission with electron populations of 10^7, while its emission pattern at various frequencies suggests an oblique rotator model with an axis of inclination. Additionally, we explore the possibility that emission originates from a disk surrounding A1, as well as from interactions between the M dwarf component and its companion, including electron acceleration at shock waves and exoplanets.

To the Neural Image Manipulation (NIM) community, a particularly pressing challenge is developing techniques for synthesizing high-quality neural images from movable materials. Unfortunately current approaches face two significant hurdles: they struggle to accommodate multiple, dynamic objects and their shadows, and they rely on pre-existing 3D models of the objects in question.

To overcome these limitations, we propose Articulated Neural Rendering (A-N-R), a novel method that employs a new transfer function to model complex, non-metallic objects. Our approach takes two primary inputs: neural images and their corresponding transmission maps, which facilitate the rendering of both dynamic objects and environmental backgrounds. Through a step-by-step process, our method reconstructs multiple surface locations on our virtual objects, which are then fitted to a simple geometric shape to make the learning process more efficient.

Compared to previous techniques, our approach achieves remarkable improvements in several key metrics: it boasts faster convergence times and the ability to fit more intricate shapes; our transmission maps exhibit significantly higher quality and accuracy; our synthesized neural images demonstrate notable enhancements in their overall quality.

Human beings can identify objects regardless of significant image distortion.
In contrast, conventional artificial neural networks struggle with such distorted images.
This paper presents a study utilizing an elastic mannequin to transform rigid objects into flexible versions, which are then utilized to train an artificial neural network to recognize objects on deformable surfaces.
It investigates the optimal position and amount for applying distortions that maximize the performance of a distorted object recognition model.
Moreover, the paper discusses the implications of these findings in the context of distortions that occur during manual manipulation.

Chern-Simons theory's path-integral for anyons is influenced by the q-deformed SU(2) symmetry, specifically relating to the Askey-Wilson algebra. By considering a Chern-Simons gauge group SU(2) with an offset, Chern-Simons path-intolgs can be associated with the representation of the Askey-Wilson algebra within its SU(2) complement. Specifically, certain Wilson loops, denoted as the Casimir-Charge (Q_cc), serve as generators for this algebra. This connection allows us to consider anyons composed of these Wilson loops, resulting in the creation of anyonic particles that exhibit properties of both fermions and bosons. These unique anyons can be utilized in the construction of non-local, anyonic chiral anyons.

The basis choice profoundly affects the magnitude of the quantum Monte Carlo sign problem at finite temperature, and in many-body problems with spatial gaps, substantial overestimation often occurs when using the natural orbital basis. We contend that the basis choice significantly influences calculations in terms of intermediate quantities. By using a basis tailored to these quantities in Fock space rather than solving the full many-body problem, the sign problem is mitigated. This approach is demonstrated in a strong-coupling spin-1/2 Hubbard model that exhibits a magnetically ordered antiferromagnet ground state. Employing a basis derived from a cluster mean-field theory with dimer corrections and a trimer-based perturbation theory substantially decreases the sign problem in high-density regimes where non-analytic behavior arises in Monte Carlo calculations. We also demonstrate that this method allows for simulation of stronger coupling limits where the sign problem is negligible. By comparing our results with exact diagonalization data in four dimensions and conventional QMC calculations utilizing a real-space basis, we confirm that certain features of mean-file theories remain reliable indicators even in their region of theoretical validity. This suggests that such methods may have broader applications in describing complex many-body phenomena.

Recent breakthroughs in language models have led to remarkable advancements in visual and auditory understanding using zero-shot techniques alone. Despite varying architectures, models exhibit comparable performance across most benchmarks, suggesting room for further investigation. By extending our analysis to numerous new benchmarks, we discovered that the number of parameters in language models significantly impacts their performance. Larger models tend to achieve higher scores on certain benchmarks, while smaller models show improved results on others. Furthermore, individual model characteristics, such as parameterization method and pre-training objectives, influence zero-shot performance differently. We explored the notion of domain alignment, suggesting a new approach to evaluating models' ability to generalize to target domains across various benchmarks.

In this research, we have established 95% confidence level exclusion limits for the parameter space of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, specifically focusing on the Higgs boson mass parameters and Higgs mixing angle. We utilized Higgs data from the latest LHC analyses, along with electroweak precision data, to determine our exclusion limits, which are applicable regardless of the supersymmetric mass spectrum. Our results indicate that current LHC searches have eliminated the region of the parameter space that could support a strong first-order phase transition in Higgs field evolution, implying that future experiments may be necessary to detect this phenomenon, such as baryogenesis through sphaleron processes, due to current searches' inability to constrain the required loss of subdominant dimension-five operator contribution to Higgs potential, particularly when Higgs mixing angles are small.

The ALMA project is set to significantly enhance the availability of reliable redshift data for galaxy studies in the period of 2 < z < 4, specifically through the use of spectral lines and photometric estimates in scenarios like deep galaxy surveys and the ALMA-GALA project. In this research, we have analyzed how effective the method of detecting redshifts is when the ALMA project is utilized. A set of 100 galaxies with known redshifts, spanning from z = 2.0 to 4.5, was obtained from the SDSS database and the COSMOS survey. A new set of CO line sensitivity and detection likelihoods was calculated for each galaxy, using a standardized observation configuration. In the resulting findings, we have found that approximately 50% of galaxies with z > 3.0 have CO line sensitivity of less than 3 Jy/km/s, and 50% of all galaxies have a CO line detection potential of 20% or more. In the event that a CO line is not detected, a robust photometric estimation of the galaxy's dust mass is set to facilitate the subsequent derivation of star formation rates, star densities, and galaxy star formation rates via a power-law model. In the resulting findings, we have found that approximately 50% of galaxies with z > 3.0 have a CO line detection of less than 3 Jy/km/s and can be used to estimate their

We introduce a novel approach using electric and magnetic response theory to investigate multipoles in quantum many-body systems. This theory allows us to calculate multipoles to any order using systematic rules. To demonstrate its effectiveness, we analyze the magnetic response of a Dirac multipole, a unique 3rd magnetic multipoles with magnetic dipole and quadrupole moments. This analysis reveals how low-lying excitations in Dirac spin liquid phases lead to large magnetic responses, providing an in-depth understanding of their characteristics, supported by recent experiments.

The breaking of symmetries in lattice systems is investigated with a new, explicit approach to breaking the conservation of cyclic magnetization in 1D and 24-site lattices under random potentials, as described by a generalized complex nonlinearity and the generalized non-Hermitian Hopfield model. Our results show that the breaking of Z3 symmetry is not instantaneous, but rather depends on the number of temporal sites in the lattice, demonstrating partial recovery of Z3 symmetry as it increases. On a 1D lattice, partial restoration of Z3 symmetry also leads to a transition from a localized to a band state. Our findings are verified through numerical simulations and an analytical approach.

A novel chemical approach, specifically a water-based method, to create Cr$_2$Al$_2$ with the non-centrosymmetric task vector structure of Mn$_2$Au has not yet been achieved. Following a thorough examination of its magnetic and magnetoelectric relationships, Cr$_2$Al$_3$ was discovered to exhibit similar characteristics to Mn$_2$Au but with unique features. Unlike the case with Mn$_2$Au, the magnetic order within Cr$_2$Al exhibits a rotation of 90 degrees, while the magnetic interactions produce an anisotropy energy of 1.5 kJ per mole, resulting in a significant magnetic anisotropy direction difference of 90 degrees. Additionally, the magnetic interactions exhibit a significant in-plane, long-range, and fractional magnitude that is 0.4 times larger than the one present in the case with Mn$_2$Au. The findings suggest that the magnetic interactions within Cr$_2$Al exhibit a relatively low susceptibility to structural disorder, given that the same level of structural disorder would lead to a phase transition in the case with Mn$_2$Au.

In this study, we investigate the application of the $\upsilon$-model, a simplified kinetic model, to simulate rarefied micro-flows with different boundary conditions. Using the Bhatnagar-Gross-Pekarek (BGP) linearized kinetic model, we assess the accuracy of the $\upsilon$-model in boundary interactions. This model is then applied to benchmark simulations for various canonical rarefied micro-flows, including thermal transpiration and the Helmholtz coil, with thermal nonequilibrium taken into account. Our results reveal that the thermal transpiration theorems derived by the $\upsilon$-model exhibit improved agreement with direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) and other kinetic simulations, including those based on solving the Boltzmann equation, especially at higher levels of rarefaction. Moreover, the $\upsilon$-model performs well in other tests, including flow through a long micro-channel, micro-channel heat sinks, and the Helmholtz coil, with or without considering the non-linear coupling between temperature and velocity.

This paper presents NoParse, a novel semantic parsing approach that bypasses the need for annotated data, thereby significantly enhancing few-shot parsing capabilities. By employing WorldScript 17, we demonstrate improved few-shot parsing performance over traditional methods that rely on annotated data. NoParse leverages a pre-trained Transformer model, which is trained on diverse Internet text data using contrastive training objectives, to supervise the alignment of semantic frames and WorldScript 17's argument labels. Additionally, the work delves into pre-training language models specifically tailored to domain-specific tasks like semantic parsing, exploring the effectiveness of training on corpus-like texts versus annotated examples.

The High Energy Physics community's existing trackless vertexing ALIEN detectors used a cryogenic process due to their two-layer design, which included Silicon Pixel and Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor layers. The addition of these cryo-PAPS detectors to tracking systems significantly boosts the system's track-hunting and angular resolution capabilities. The cryo-PAPS technology, however, is no longer applicable to future experiments due to its outdated architecture. The AC coupled low gain avalanche Diode development has been a successful alternative, with its AC coupled variant already incorporated into several experiments. Recent advancements in AC-APS technology involved transitioning from high resistivity in-fusion oxide nitride, which had been used previously, to highly resistive p-type silicon through a careful doping process. The reduced capacitance achieved with the thinner oxide and the improved charge transfer from the AC-APS demonstrate notable advancements in this field.

Using the Norwegian Einstein Public Survey, which observed low-mass active galactic nuclei in the 0.05 < z < 0.1 range with the MAXI mission, we found a target, 2XMM J123103.2+110648, showing notable X-ray variations. The source was observed multiple times by XMM-Newton, displaying a complex pattern of hard X-ray flares, likely associated with flares in accretion disks. Furthermore, we detected X-ray activity extending into the soft band, indicating possible changes in X-ray timing properties. Our findings demonstrate that X-ray timing studies in the 0.1 < z < 1.0 range are feasible using the Einstein Public Survey and can reveal significant insights into low-mass accretion processes.

We've conducted a groundbreaking study of Cool White Dwarfs in the Large Magellanic Cloud using the James Webb Space Telescope, specifically the NIRCam. By cross-referencing with data from Gaia, HST, VISTA, and HSCSS, we've identified 104 B-type magnetic stars in the LMC. Our analysis of four of these magnetic stars with extended data from HST enables us to detect their magnetic fields. In addition, we've detected or confirmed the existence of magnetospheres in 13 of these O and B-type stars, including 7 that are new discoveries. We've also found a correlation between the rotation periods of these stars and their surrounding magnetic fields. Based on our findings, we've concluded that the magnetospheres in these fast-rotating O and B-type Dwarfs are likely a byproduct of their rotation speeds. We've also discovered a significant number of supersoft X-ray sources in the LMC, including four that are new discoveries. Furthermore, we've found that the light curves of these stars are irregular, but some of them exhibit variability on timescales of about 200 days. We've also found a connection between the rotation periods of these stars and their magnetic fields, which aligns with our expectations. In a separate study, we've found that the rotation periods of these stars are consistent with our expectations. One-dimensional oscillator observations can be seen as examples of intertwining operators. The connections between two oscillators with differing mass and potential parameters can be established through a pair of intertwining operators that satisfy a specific differential equation, which is the Schrödinger equation for one of the oscillators. This established relationship enables the calculation of the scattering matrix for any set of parameters. Moreover, when considering a transition between a harmonic oscillator and a free particle system, the correspondence rules for the path integral can be simplified, reducing to a single integral kernel that describes the propagator of a free particle, which can be derived from a path integral for a harmonic oscillator involving a specific choice of parameters.

In a sample of 15 galaxies with low to moderate metallicity and irregular types, we've studied the relationship between star formation rates (SFR) derived from infrared and optical data. Using SFR infrared calibration, we found that our sample exhibits significant scatter in the correlation between SFR infrared and SFR H30. This suggests that a substantial portion (up to 50%) of the total infrared radiation in these galaxies is not attributable to dust emission resulting from star formation. We've also found evidence that the traditional star formation rate calibrations based on H30, which work well for solar metallicity galaxies, may not accurately represent lower metallicity galaxies. This is attributed to the fact that in these lower metallicity galaxies, the star formation rates derived from H30 tend to overestimate the true star formation rates by a factor of 2.3 on average. This is largely due to the H30 emission being significantly affected by the H2 emission, which is itself associated with the bulk of dust emission. This indicates that the traditional H30 calibrations, which are based on the assumption that the H2 emission is directly proportional to the dust emission, may need to be revised to account for the complexities introduced by the lower metallicity galaxies.

There are two distinct types of non-trivially virtually cyclic groups that arise from minimal, continuous actions on Hausdorff topological spaces: (1) groups virtually isomorphic to the circle group S, and (2) the infinite dihedral group D_inf. D_inf can be expressed as a closed subgroup in both the group of circle rotations (under composition) and in a suitable convex subset of the real numbers consisting of points 0 and n+1/2 for any integer n. Our investigation involves classifying all closed D-inf subgroups within a Hausdorff topological space.

Innonlinear model order reduction, non-local and globally continuous approaches are vital. Recently, the number of uses of collocation-based and kernal-based methods for model order reduction has increased, as they can offer a more accurate and faster converging alternative to classical Galerkin methods. Our research explores whether non-local problems can be effectively solved using locally continuous Galerkin projections. We investigate the capabilities of Galerkin projections and their ability to match both data and the residual, and how the choice of projection method affects the quality and convergence of reduced models, the stability of reduced systems, and the accuracy and convergence rates of reduced models. We compare Galerkin projections to collocation-based and kernel-based methods in a comprehensive numerical experiment.

This work develops a novel observer structure, optimizing estimator performance in real-time. By leveraging linearization techniques, the method generates accurate state estimates for complex nonlinear systems, such as deterministic epidemic models, with limited measurement data. Our implementation focuses on the SIR epidemic model using Seaborn in Python, highlighting the practical application of the method. Utilizing local linearization techniques, the method achieves optimal estimates of system states despite incomplete data. Our results demonstrate significant speed improvements over existing observers, particularly when measuring only the "S" variable, with acceleration factors of 1.5 to 2 times. Furthermore, by adjusting the observer gain parameters based on measurement frequencies, the method optimizes convergence. This research exemplifies the practical utility of the method in biological systems.

Temporal knowledge graphs and their corresponding embeddings have gained significant attention in recent years due to their importance in understanding entities' behaviors and event occurrences over time. Despite advancements in temporal knowledge graph embeddings, a notable gap exists between them and the well-established methods used for static graphs. To bridge this disparity, we introduce a novel approach that leverages LSTM networks to capture time patterns in entity types, in relation to other entities and time frames. This strategy is grounded in the assumption that entities of the same category exhibit similar temporal behaviors. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our method surpasses the current state-of-the-art temporal embedding models and also outperforms various static embedding algorithms.

For single-mode Kerr-lens mode-locking to occur in a laser system, the intricate balance between the mode-locking effect and the lens's aperture effect must be achieved. Specifically, there should be no impact on lens-aperture enabled Kerr-loop switching when the mode-locking effect causes changes in the lens's focal length. However, most existing Kerr-lens mode-locking lasers exhibit instability in their pulse-to-pulse focal lengths, particularly due to thermal instability in the lens material itself. To resolve this issue, we developed a novel approach to achieve mode-locking stability in a Ku-band microdisk laser by incorporating a lens into the Kerr-lens aperture and utilizing in-lens electro-thermal modulation. This innovative design ensures mode-locking stability not just along a single operating line, but across an extensive parameter range, significantly enhancing mode-locking stability compared to prior art. This new strategy has significant implications for improving mode-locking stability in similar devices, notably in solid-state mode-locking lasers.

In asynchronous online federated learning, a central federated server manages client registration and training sessions. The framework efficiently utilizes idle client groups to train newly admitted clients. This paper explores the impact of data transmission efficiency on asynchronous online federated learning and proposes a novel model where the benefits of partial data sharing among participants to foster competition. The optimization problem is formulated, and the first-order optimality conditions for the optimal allocation strategy are derived. The condition for the existence of a unique equilibrium is also identified and demonstrated through numerical experiments.

We examine silicon film photonic crystal absorbers with a photonic crystal back mirror and a thin silicon layer, and thick silicon layer configurations. In our model, light is simulated using a 2D FDTD method, and we study how these absorbers absorb light and reflect it based on the thickness of the silicon film and the lattice constant of the photonic crystal. When using a thick silicon layer and a certain lattice constant, the photonic crystal absorbs light and suppresses reflection at specific wavelengths, which is useful in thin film applications. In contrast, thin silicon film samples enable high absorption but low reflectivity at specific wavelengths, which is useful in thick film applications. When using a thick silicon layer, the photonic crystal reflects light over a wide range of wavelengths, and when using a thin silicon film, the sample reflects light over a narrow range of wavelengths.

Two specific functions, defined based on relationships with integers, are central to understanding the dynamics of the exponential map in complex plane when considering hyperbolic invariant curves beneath the real axis.

We develop a new theory of high-dimensional expanders that encompasses various concepts such as spectral expanders, and we derive properties that indicate their potential in computational applications. This includes the construction of high-dimensional expander locally correct codes and the formulation of efficient PCPs of proximity. Furthermore, our research provides a detailed examination of the connection between random walks on expander graphs and their high-dimensional counterparts, specifically the interaction between local and global exploration on oriented graphs.

The properties of the Gd$^{3+}$ ion in GdInO$_3$ are being studied through the use of a Gd$^{153}$-NMR spectrometer with 14% enrichment of the Gd isotope. Research was conducted at temperatures of 4.2 K and 297 K under strong magnetic fields ranging from 2 T to 20 T. We found that GdInO$_3$ is an orthorhombic lattice with Gd$^{3+}$ ions having sites that are not symmetric. The different environments that Gd$^{3+}$ ions experience affect how they interact with magnetic fields, resulting in different ion frequencies. The frequency of the Gd$^{3+}$ ion at 4.2 K and 20 T field is 138.6 MHz. The different interactions between the Gd$^{3+}$ ion and surrounding nuclei cause distortion in the NMR spectrum as magnetic field strength increases. The distortion is mainly due to interactions between the Gd$^{3+}$ ion and nearby protons. The distortion also reveals a broad range of possible nuclear transitions in GdInO$_3$.

The process of node representation in graph-based methods involves capturing a node's context, but existing methods that summarize neighbor relationships via the Sum of Normalized H-order Adjacency Matrix (SNHAM) are hindered by issues of representation redundancy in sparse networks. To resolve these shortcomings, we propose a novel approach that involves selecting a subset of neighbors through cardinality restriction to generate a more efficient and contextualized representation in sparse graphs. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we integrate it into popular graph neural networks, such as GNRS and GCRF, and evaluate its performance across various domains, including classification in sparse networks and recommendation systems. Experimental outcomes indicate significant improvements over existing methods, with gains observed even when incorporating dense networks, and code along with detailed models are publicly available for further investigation.

A novel, efficient design for pill activation, known as the drop activation method,
has gained popularity, yet its underlying physics, specifically activation via a
liquid drop, remains poorly understood. To address this, we study the vapor
generation process when a water drop is placed on an encapsulated pill, 
utilizing an integrated sensor and high-speed imaging techniques. 
Furthermore, we enhance efficiency by developing a two-room setup for the drop
activation, which enables us to refine the vapor density within chamber X and 
improve measurements taken from it.

A mathematical model for non-linear interference (NLI) has been presented in an earlier paper. This model applies to a broad spectrum of multi-dimensional non-linear interference scenarios, including those that are polarisation-multiplexed. In the case of format-specific non-linear interference, such as non-linear phase rotation and Raman gain, the model provides an accurate prediction of system performance. A new model for standard non-linear interference that takes polarisation-multiplexing into account is introduced, along with generalized expressions that can accommodate arbitrary dimensional multiplexing. Additionally, a different expression is offered to estimate the standard NLI in systems using coherent detection.

To create a unified image incorporating diverse visual information from multiple sources including distinct modalities, a novel fusion method is proposed, utilizing deep learning-based pixel alignment and dynamic channel weighting in a end-to-end approach. The feasibility of this novel fusion method is tested in two essential applications: detecting fires and extracting fires from multiple image fusion. The findings indicate that the proposed method outperforms traditional fusion techniques and certain state-of-the-art deep learning-based approaches. The primary benefits of this method are its ability to enhance the readability of multiple image sets and its use in fire detection and extraction. The proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques with improved results of up to 14% and 19%, respectively, under two different evaluation metrics.

Automated mental health diagnosis based on social media data is emerging as a
promising approach, and existing methods show promising accuracy for diagnosing
depression. In contrast, the diagnostic accuracy of social media data for other mental
health conditions remains unclear, and our study sheds light on its potential and
limitations. Our objective is to enhance automated diagnosis by leveraging social media
data and improving the diagnostic clarity of mental health conditions. Our proposed
solution utilizes language models and a specific social media data approach. Our findings
reveal that social media data can provide accurate diagnoses, albeit less precise than data
collected from clinical settings, and showcase specific conditions such as depression,
bipolar disorder, anxiety, and PTSD can be effectively diagnosed using this method.

Our research model examines how to minimize the final number of people infected with SARS-CoV-2 through a combination of private hospital and institute strategies, and government-implemented lockdown measures. The effectiveness of individual and collective actions is evaluated within the context of a cellular automaton and a network-based compartmental epidemic model, which also accounts for individual hospital capacity and testing capabilities. The outcomes of our study show that the interaction between the slow spread characteristics of the virus and private hospital/institute strategies, particularly those focused on testing and isolation, can significantly impact the need for lockdown measures and minimize infection rates. The outcomes of our model indicate a substantial difference in performance between centralized and decentralized hospital and institute management, revealing the substantial impact of private sector engagement in disease control. The outcomes of our model provide insights and recommendations to policymakers and health officials on the importance of private sector engagement and coordination in the effective management and control of infectious diseases.

Theoretical studies of nuclear resonances have a long history, dating back to the 1950s. Researchers have focused on how different types of giant resonances interact with each other and how they change when moving from spherical to deformed nuclei. This involves analyzing how these resonances couple with different multipole vibrations, such as quadrupole and octupole, and how their interactions can either raise or lower their energies. Our work uses the Hartree-Fock-Random-Phase Approximation to model how giant resonances interact in different nuclear regions. Our results are in line with previous studies that have used more complex theoretical and experimental methods.

We investigate frequency-domain characteristics of nonlinear feedback control loops that incorporate a central stiction zone of width $2h$ within the actuator movement range. The system includes a rigid mass, a restoring spring, and a dashpot, with the actuator movement limited by the stiction zone's width. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for a stroboscopic map to have fixed points at any stiction width $h$, demonstrating how the stiction map's nature and potential for limit cycles are influenced by this width. We identify specific stiction widths that can cause asymmetrical crossing of fixed points and width intervals allowing arbitrarily small stiction values to induce crossing at any desired map map location. We further develop stability and stability margin criteria for an order-$m$ Sticks-N-Sticks (SNS) motion to remain stable or become unstable. Additionally, we create sufficient conditions for an order-$k$ Spikes-N-Spikes (Spikes-N-Spikes: Spikes motion) to exist, where $k\leq m$, and show how increasing the stiction width can cause the system to stick to the stiction zone and come to a halt, contrasting with a space filling curve like a generalized Van der Corput sequence that covers its $[-1,1]$ domain without a stiction zone.

The behavior of current trading mechanisms continues to puzzle researchers, particularly concerning inconsistent effects of trading frictions. Past studies using idealized models cannot adequately explain this phenomenon. This work utilizes the idealized World of Financial Agents to investigate the combined influence of costs and liquidity restrictions on financial strategy performance. An evaluation of existing strategies reveals a strong correlation between profits and trading costs but an unexpected reduction in liquidity limits' effect beyond certain thresholds.

In recent years, deep learning-based recommendation systems have significantly
improved user engagement by delivering tailored content. However, their
recommendations often fail to fully deliver an optimal experience, largely
because users' intentions are complex and frequently ambiguous. Building upon
our past research, which laid the groundwork for neural network user recommendation
models, this study delves into the user's mind to enhance the overall
experience. By employing clustering techniques, precise user intent can be
identified, allowing for iterative refinement of user models and ultimately
leading to noticeable user experience enhancements, as demonstrated in
experiments on real-world data for both CTR and dwell time.

Reducible double confluent Heun equations can be solved using an adapted version of the Fok-Goncharov transformation, a technique originally used for the hypergeometric equation, in combination with a method of series that is applicable to the single confluent Heun equation. We demonstrate a method for generating holomorphic solutions to a class of reducible double confluent Heun equations that adhere to specific parameter values. The solution is a Laurent power series that incorporates coefficients derived from the solutions to the corresponding single confluent Heun equation. We also provide generic conditions for a non-trivial reduction of the single confluent Heun equation in order to obtain a solution that is applicable throughout the entire complex plane with a single singularity.

Low-rank matrix recovery is a crucial task in various scientific fields. A recent study found that PCA applied to a low-rank matrix formed from the sum of multiple data matrices is effective in recovering the low-rank matrix, even when the data matrices have the same dimensions and are scaled uniformly. This research extends the application of this result to semi-supervised learning problems, specifically for 1-means and principal component analysis in contexts with noise outliers. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that when handling non-outlier data with uneven class distributions or outlier dimensions, PCA on weighted combinations of data with proportional class sizes and no covariances yields the same asymptotic performance as PCA applied to the aggregated matrix.

Our research has revealed that fractionalized boundary states can originate from classical systems, even when they lack half-linear symmetry. This occurs because the presence of a half-linear symmetry is not a prerequisite for the emergence of such states. Instead, it has been established that a clique of half-modes is sufficient, provided that some of these fractions align. Our findings have been validated through theoretical examples and an experiment using a 1D spin chain, which demonstrated the classical origin of a boundary state. This outcome holds significant implications for the precise targeting and creation of topological states.

To effectively detect transitions in $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ that are not allowed by SM predictions and potentially caused by new physics affecting lepton flavour universality, it's crucial to study multiple decay pathways, such as muon and electron production. Our analysis of the LHCb detector data from 7 TeV $p_p$ collisions, which contains 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, reveals J/$\psi$ $\to$ $\mu^+ \mu^-$ and J/$\psi$ $\to$ $e^+ e^-$ decay products originating from $B^0$, $B^0_s$, and $B^+$ candidate decays. We're searching for $B^0_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$, $B^0_s \to e^+ e^-$, $B^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$, $B^0 \to e^+ e^-$, comparing these to the predicted SM rates. Our findings indicate that $B^0_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ is not detected, but rather is bounded at 7.7$\times 10^{-10}$ with 95% confidence. While the measured rate is in agreement with the predicted SM rate, it is 2.5 standard deviations below the expectation of 3.0$\times 10

In this study, a large-scale networked system is modeled as a collection of interconnected agents, each controlled by a specific input variable, with the objective of synchronizing these controllers over a specified time period. To achieve this goal, a distributed controller synchronization algorithm based on a 1-norm constraint is developed, incorporating a distributed model predictive control framework and a continuous coupling mechanism inspired by distributed exponential stability techniques. Additionally, a continuous coupling term with locally supported support is integrated to enhance the controller synchronization algorithm's stability, thus increasing its resilience to the impact of network-based communication topologies. Utilizing a distributed model predictive control framework, the designed algorithm ensures real-time feasibility by solving sub-problems locally at each agent and updating the controllers through an adaptive coupling mechanism. Specifically, the proposed algorithm incorporates a continuous coupling mechanism based on the $\ell_1$-norm that ensures the convergence of controllers to a neighborhood of each other, with the size of this neighborhood directly dependent on the network's communication topology. Furthermore, the algorithm's computational efficiency and feasibility are supported by an iterative coupling mechanism, with the size of the computational problem associated with each sub-problem depending solely on the size of the individual agent system state-space rather than the overall size of the networked system. Ultimately, the convergence of the designed algorithm to a neighborhood of each other is rigorously established, along with the design of an adaptive coupling mechanism that ensures the resilience of the algorithm to the impact of the network-based communication topologies. Furthermore,

Our novel computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) framework is specifically designed to pinpoint and classify the most severe cases of COVID-19 through automated CT scan analysis. Our approach leverages three key components to achieve this goal: 1) a content-aware image disassembly module to pinpoint the most crucial content within an image, 2) an attention mechanism to aggregate image features across multiple scales, and 3) an abnormality localization module to aggregate image features across multiple modalities. Our advanced framework excels in both image classification and bounding box localization tasks, surpassing state-of-the-art methods and yielding a impressive 98.33% accuracy on our validation dataset and 94.33% accuracy on the test dataset.

This code contributes a user-friendly collection of sophisticated analytic tools for advanced linear analysis in complex network research. It specifically supports advanced studies on random matrix and localization analysis related to complex networks. The code features robust functions for generating extensive data sets on various complex network models. These include RMT ensembles characterized by different spinoff and return probabilities for preferential attachment networks. Furthermore, the code includes algorithmic implementations of key operators and additional utilities for parameter estimation. These encompass mean and covariance operator estimation derived from spectral embedding and neighbor-based covariance estimation. Lastly, the code offers additional tools for deepening mathematical understanding and facilitating numerical experiments. These tools include the estimation of the Stochastic Kernel operator from empirical data and single-vector power iteration algorithms.

We suggest that the connection between an organism's ecology and evolution is influenced by two primary variables: temperature and mutagen sensitivity. These variables dictate whether ecological and evolutionary processes occur in an sequential manner, with one necessitating the other, or occur concurrently in a combined feedback loop. We incorporate these principles into an model system that combines cellular ecology with mitochondrial evolution and apply them to examine real-world ecosystems across different geographical areas. For each tested location, we calculate the timeframes for ecological and evolutionary changes using a ecodynamic model and a population dynamic model and compare the results to observed data on species diversity across different scales.

This paper examines how speech representation models can be manipulated by malicious actors with limited knowledge, by assessing their susceptibility to "zero-knowledge" attacks. The study analyzes the resilience of speech models against two types of attacks - speech attacks and text attacks - designed to degrade their performance when exposed to adversarial examples. Our results show that speech-based representation models are more vulnerable to manipulation from adversaries with knowledge of the model's inner workings, while speech models based on word pieces and character tokens within the speaker identification task appear to be less susceptible to manipulation by adversaries with limited knowledge.

Automated Market Makers in liquidity pools can be manipulated by large investors, known as whales, for their own benefit. The order of the non-linear pricing function in these market makers is a debated issue, and it's currently unknown how this affects the outcomes for investors. Our research, however, delves into this issue by assuming the order $p$ in the curve. Specifically, we focus on the Uniswap-style market mechanism and its order $p=3$. Our key findings include the following: 1) Curving the pricing function in a certain way leads to greater investor surplus compared to linear pricing. 2) In contrast, curving the pricing function in a different way creates opportunities for profitable arbitrage. 3) In contrast to previous research, our results show that the outcomes can actually benefit the liquidity providers. Our study also includes numerical examples to support our findings.

This research develops an Oaxaca-like decomposition framework to investigate the influence of observables on causal inferences in the presence of uncertainty. Building upon the CCA algorithm by Bowers et al. (2020), which utilizes Oaxaca-like decomposition for unique Oaxaca-like decomposition trees that bound causal inferences with missing data, our framework applies this concept to quantifying the stability of causal inferences when sensitive variables are missing. We demonstrate the utility of our approach through a simulation study using the National Longitudinal Surveys, where we examine how "training" Oaxaca-like decomposition trees based on specific variables impacts PSMD and treatment effect estimates. Furthermore, we showcase the applicability of our approach in the context of analyzing COVID-19 vaccination behaviors among U.S. citizens by causal treatment effect and PSMD.

We examine the various $\operatorname{U_q(\mathsf{sl}_2)}$-symmetries for the quantum plane and prove that these symmetries, along with their $K_{\pm 1}$ actions, exhaust all possible actions of the Hopf algebra $\operatorname{U_q(\mathsf{sl}_2)}$ on the quantum plane that are module isomorphisms from its antipode to itself. The specific $\operatorname{U_q(\mathsf{sl}_2)}$-symmetries under consideration are all possible conjugations, and also all the actions are determinate based on their quantum group antipode behavior.

Emerging technologies like Blockchain and Edge Computing hold great promise for transforming V2X applications in next-generation ISDV systems. This study delves into the potential of Blockchain-enabled Edge Computing architecture to enhance data exchange between vehicles and services within intelligent transportation frameworks. By leveraging the benefits of these technologies, V2X systems can significantly boost security, privacy, and interoperability. Our research examines the performance implications of such architectures through simulations grounded in real-world traffic conditions. This investigation sheds light on the optimal deployment strategies for Blockchain and Edge Computing technologies in enhancing traffic management, safety, and comfort in vehicular networks.

Measurements of the fragmentation fraction of parton-level charm and beauty quarks into specific D0 and DPi0 mesons are presented. These measurements are based on data collected from LHCb detector events involving proton-proton collisions at a specific energy level. The fragmentation fraction measurement is particularly useful in understanding the parton-level charm and beauty quark production rates in proton-proton collisions. These measurements also allow for comparisons with theoretical models, other measured values, and various observables.

We aim to develop a cryogenic platform featuring a 1.5 meters by 1 meters by 1 meter experimental volume, equipped with minimum movement capabilities, in our darkroom setting at INFN-Frascati, to enable the investigation of new physics phenomena beyond the Standard Model using quantum sensors. This cryogenic system will enable the precise measurement of magnetic fields and an enhanced, high-performance RF readout of spin qubit systems through the use of quantum sensing technologies. By integrating these technologies, inferring gravitational parameters through the spin-gravity interaction will become feasible, with potential dimensionality reduction of data from our quantum sensors. We aim to increase the sensitivity of the darkroom to T oscillating magnetic fields below 10^-24 T/Hz^0.5 in the 1-100 Hz frequency range through the unique combination of RF readout and magnetic shielding technologies.

Many Python crypto libraries are susceptible to misuse due to their unique API design, although the extent to which developers actually misuse these libraries in practice is not fully understood. Therefore, this research aims to investigate how API design influences crypto library usage by comparing the results of a large-scale analysis of over 100,000 Java and C programs utilizing a different set of secure coding standards, to their Python counterparts, using a similar code finding methodology. The study's findings indicate that, on average, Python crypto library usage patterns resemble those of Java and C more closely than previously anticipated, with over 60% of Python programs utilizing safe crypto functions. Furthermore, this research examines the causes of secure coding standard violations in Java and C, and identifies distinct patterns of secure coding standard violations within Python programs.

A novel approach, referred to as Self-3D, is proposed to recover the three-dimensional structure of large scenes from substantial amounts of two-dimensional image data. In large-scale scenarios, the second 3D moment can be accurately reconstructed after a single batch processing step, whereas the moment tensor requires multiple steps due to the limited information in images. To address this challenge, the proposed method employs a variational optimization strategy guided by external prior information to refine the reconstruction process. The cost function of each step is derived from intermediate three-dimensional models, contrasting with the method of deep learning approaches, which recover three-dimensional structures based on pretrained two-dimensional features. The cost function is minimized using two techniques: the first utilizes self-supervision through three-dimensional occlusion and reassembly, and the second leverages occlusion prior information to optimize energy minimization. The cost functions are compatible with both voxel and mesh-based representations, which enables robust three-dimensional structure reconstruction. The results of the experiments demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method in recovering three-dimensional structures of large-scale objects, including realistic ones, as well as the usability of two-dimensional features for three-dimensional structure reconstruction.

To solve the problem of recovering subsurface reflection coefficients from seismic data, a comprehensive data-based objective function is established, and its relationship to the conventional reflection coefficient synthesis method is explored. By incorporating the concepts of non-convex synthesis sparse models and 1-D atomic decomposition, an innovative and effective approach called C1-RCs is established. This method can accurately recover multiwave reflection coefficients with various interference patterns, even in the presence of overfitting issues. A constrained finite slowness transformation is applied to control the shape of the reflection coefficients, and the convergence of the proposed algorithm is theoretically proven. Additionally, a corresponding OASIS-SIM forward modeling approach is developed, and its efficiency and accuracy are demonstrated through a common offset single station data set, a common offset double station data set, and a 2-D data set recorded by the Marmosi model.
For a symbol in $A_\omega(-1,1)$, we determine the compact and weakly compact conditions of $T_g$ on $BMOA_\alpha$ for $1 < \alpha < 2$.

Our research reveals how overlaps of low-energy wavefunctions in spin chains with conformal symmetry at their critical point can exactly determine central charge, subleading log coefficients, and subleading terms of the entropy scaling relation. These findings are supported by analytical proofs and numerical validations using magnetization profiles and with applications to spin chains exhibiting ferromagnetic long-range order and analog systems of fermions.

A novel set-valued tagging strategy is presented for part-of-speech tagging tasks.
This innovative approach amplifies the tagging tagger's effectiveness in anticipating
established tags for unrecognized words within the testing dataset, by maintaining a
slightly lower performance for known tags. We propose an algorithm for generating
an optimized set-valued tagger using existing feature-based tagging methods.
Experiments conducted on the Penn Treebank dataset showcase the effectiveness of
this strategy.
